title: The Seed of the Woman (The Protoevangelium)

ot.author: Moses
ot.context: God's judgment against the serpent in Eden following the Fall.
ot.text: And I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed. He will crush your head, and you will strike his heel.”
ot.keyPhrase: He will crush your head, and you will strike his heel

nt.author: Paul / John
nt.context: Paul promises that God will soon crush Satan; in John's vision the dragon, 'that ancient serpent', is thrown down and makes war on the woman's children.
nt.text: The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you. … And the great dragon was hurled down—that ancient serpent called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world. He was hurled to the earth, and his angels with him. … And the dragon was enraged at the woman, and went to make war with the rest of her children, who keep the commandments of God and hold to the testimony of Jesus. And the dragon stood on the shore of the sea.
nt.keyPhrase: will soon crush Satan under your feet

bridge: After the Fall, God tells the serpent there will be enmity (lasting hostility) between its offspring and the woman's: 'He will crush your head, and you will strike his heel.' Since the early centuries Christians have read this as the first announcement of the gospel, often called the Protoevangelium ('first gospel'): a promise that a descendant of Eve would defeat evil at the cost of his own suffering; many see the struck heel as the cross. The New Testament never quotes the verse, but it echoes it. Paul writes, 'The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet.' Revelation calls the dragon 'that ancient serpent' and shows him at war with 'the rest of her children', using the same Greek word for offspring that the Greek Old Testament uses in Genesis 3:15.

title: Blessing to All Nations Through Abraham's Seed

ot.author: Moses
ot.context: After Isaac is spared on a mountain in the land of Moriah, God renews His covenant promise to Abraham.
ot.text: And through your offspring all nations of the earth will be blessed, because you have obeyed My voice.”
ot.keyPhrase: through your offspring all nations of the earth will be blessed

nt.author: Paul / Peter (recorded by Luke)
nt.context: Paul argues that the promised 'seed' is Christ; Peter quotes the promise to a crowd at the temple in Jerusalem.
nt.text: The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed. The Scripture does not say, “and to seeds,” meaning many, but “and to your seed,” meaning One, who is Christ. … And you are sons of the prophets and of the covenant God made with your fathers when He said to Abraham, ‘Through your offspring all the families of the earth will be blessed.’
nt.keyPhrase: Through your offspring all the families of the earth will be blessed

bridge: After testing Abraham with Isaac, God promises that 'through your offspring all nations of the earth will be blessed'. Two New Testament passages take up this promise. In Acts 3:25 Peter quotes it to a crowd at the temple and tells them they are 'sons of the prophets and of the covenant'. In Galatians 3:16 Paul argues that the promises say 'seed', not 'seeds', so they point to one person, Christ, through whom 'the blessing promised to Abraham would come to the Gentiles' (Galatians 3:14). The Hebrew word for seed (offspring) can mean one descendant or many, so the focus on one person is Paul's reading, which Christians have followed.

title: The Royal Scepter of Judah & Shiloh's Coming

ot.author: Jacob (recorded by Moses)
ot.context: Jacob's deathbed blessing of his twelve sons in Egypt, in which Judah is pictured as a lion and promised the scepter.
ot.text: Judah is a young lion— my son, you return from the prey. Like a lion he crouches and lies down; like a lioness, who dares to rouse him? The scepter will not depart from Judah, nor the staff from between his feet, until Shiloh comes and the allegiance of the nations is his.
ot.keyPhrase: Judah is a young lion

nt.author: John / Luke
nt.context: In John's vision of the heavenly throne room, an elder calls Jesus the Lion of the tribe of Judah; Luke's family tree of Jesus reaches back to Judah.
nt.text: Then one of the elders said to me, “Do not weep! Behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has triumphed to open the scroll and its seven seals.” … the son of Amminadab, the son of Admin, the son of Arni, the son of Hezron, the son of Perez, the son of Judah,
nt.keyPhrase: the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David

bridge: In his deathbed blessing, Jacob pictures Judah as a lion and promises that 'the scepter will not depart from Judah' until Shiloh comes. The New Testament never quotes this promise or mentions Shiloh, but Revelation 5:5 calls Jesus 'the Lion of the tribe of Judah', a title drawn from the lion image in Genesis 49:9. Luke's family tree traces Jesus back to Judah (Luke 3:33), though it says nothing about the scepter. Jewish and Christian interpreters have long read the scepter promise as pointing to the Messiah (God's promised anointed king). The word Shiloh is uncertain: it may be a name or title, or a phrase meaning the one to whom the scepter belongs, and no single reading is settled.

title: The Star Rising Out of Jacob

ot.author: Balaam (recorded by Moses)
ot.context: Balaam's fourth prophetic oracle overlooking the plains of Moab.
ot.text: I see him, but not now; I behold him, but not near. A star will come forth from Jacob, and a scepter will arise from Israel. He will crush the skulls of Moab and strike down all the sons of Sheth.
ot.keyPhrase: A star will come forth from Jacob, and a scepter will arise from Israel

nt.author: Matthew / John
nt.context: Magi from the east come to Jerusalem seeking the newborn King of the Jews, whose star they saw; in Revelation Jesus calls Himself 'the bright Morning Star'.
nt.text: asking, “Where is the One who has been born King of the Jews? We saw His star in the east and have come to worship Him.” … “I, Jesus, have sent My angel to give you this testimony for the churches. I am the Root and the Offspring of David, the bright Morning Star.”
nt.keyPhrase: We saw His star in the east

bridge: Balaam was a seer brought 'from the mountains of the east' (Numbers 23:7), hired by the king of Moab to curse Israel. Instead he foresaw a future ruler: a star from Jacob and a scepter from Israel, images of a king. Matthew does not quote this oracle, though he quotes other prophecies in the same chapter. Yet his Magi, also from the east, come seeking the newborn 'King of the Jews' whose star they saw, and many readers hear an echo of Balaam here, as they do when Jesus calls Himself 'the bright Morning Star' (Revelation 22:16). How the Magi linked a star to a Jewish king, Matthew does not say.

title: The Kinsman-Redeemer in Bethlehem's Lineage

ot.author: Samuel (trad.)
ot.context: At the town gate of Bethlehem, Boaz buys back Elimelech's land and takes Ruth as his wife; the women bless the LORD for Naomi's grandson Obed, the grandfather of David.
ot.text: At this, Boaz said to the elders and all the people, “You are witnesses today that I am buying from Naomi all that belonged to Elimelech, Chilion, and Mahlon. Moreover, I have acquired Ruth the Moabitess, Mahlon’s widow, as my wife, to raise up the name of the deceased through his inheritance, so that his name will not disappear from among his brothers or from the gate of his home. You are witnesses today.” … Then the women said to Naomi, “Blessed be the LORD, who has not left you this day without a kinsman-redeemer. May his name become famous in Israel. He will renew your life and sustain you in your old age. For your daughter-in-law, who loves you and is better to you than seven sons, has given him birth.” And Naomi took the child, placed him on her lap, and became a nurse to him. The neighbor women said, “A son has been born to Naomi,” and they named him Obed. He became the father of Jesse, the father of David.
ot.keyPhrase: they named him Obed. He became the father of Jesse, the father of David

nt.author: Matthew / Paul
nt.context: Matthew's genealogy of Jesus names Boaz, Ruth and Obed; Paul says God sent His Son, born under the law, to redeem those under the law.
nt.text: Salmon was the father of Boaz by Rahab, Boaz the father of Obed by Ruth, Obed the father of Jesse, and Jesse the father of David the king. Next: David was the father of Solomon by Uriah’s wife, … But when the time had fully come, God sent His Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those under the law, that we might receive our adoption as sons.
nt.keyPhrase: Boaz the father of Obed by Ruth, Obed the father of Jesse

bridge: Two laws stand behind Ruth 4: a close relative could buy back land a poor kinsman had sold (Leviticus 25:25), and a brother was to marry his dead brother's widow if she had no son, to carry on his name (Deuteronomy 25:5-6). Boaz, a kinsman-redeemer (Hebrew go’el, a relative with the right to redeem), combines the two: he buys Elimelech's land and marries Ruth 'to raise up the name of the deceased', though he is not the dead man's brother. The women then bless the LORD for a redeemer, most naturally the newborn Obed, David's grandfather, and Matthew lists Boaz, Ruth and Obed among Jesus' ancestors. Christians have long seen Boaz as a picture of Christ, sent 'to redeem those under the law' (Galatians 4:5), but no New Testament text makes that link.

title: God's Anointed King & The Horn of Salvation

ot.author: Hannah
ot.context: Hannah's prophetic prayer at the tabernacle in Shiloh before Israel even had a king.
ot.text: At that time Hannah prayed: “My heart rejoices in the LORD in whom my horn is exalted. My mouth speaks boldly against my enemies, for I rejoice in Your salvation. There is no one holy like the LORD. Indeed, there is no one besides You! And there is no Rock like our God. Do not boast so proudly, or let arrogance come from your mouth, for the LORD is a God who knows, and by Him actions are weighed. The bows of the mighty are broken, but the feeble are equipped with strength. The well-fed hire themselves out for food, but the starving hunger no more. The barren woman gives birth to seven, but she who has many sons pines away. The LORD brings death and gives life; He brings down to Sheol and raises up. The LORD sends poverty and wealth; He humbles and He exalts. He raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the ash heap. He seats them among princes and bestows on them a throne of honor. For the foundations of the earth are the LORD’s, and upon them He has set the world. He guards the steps of His faithful ones, but the wicked perish in darkness; for by his own strength shall no man prevail. Those who oppose the LORD will be shattered. He will thunder from heaven against them. The LORD will judge the ends of the earth and will give power to His king. He will exalt the horn of His anointed.”
ot.keyPhrase: He will exalt the horn of His anointed

nt.author: Luke (Mary's Magnificat & Zechariah)
nt.context: Mary's song after the announcement of Jesus' birth, and Zechariah's song at the birth of his son John, both echoing Hannah's prayer.
nt.text: Then Mary said: “My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit rejoices in God my Savior! For He has looked with favor on the humble state of His servant. From now on all generations will call me blessed. For the Mighty One has done great things for me. Holy is His name. His mercy extends to those who fear Him, from generation to generation. He has performed mighty deeds with His arm; He has scattered those who are proud in the thoughts of their hearts. He has brought down rulers from their thrones, but has exalted the humble. He has filled the hungry with good things, but has sent the rich away empty. He has helped His servant Israel, remembering to be merciful, as He promised to our fathers, to Abraham and his descendants forever.” … He has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of His servant David,
nt.keyPhrase: He has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of His servant David

bridge: Hannah's prayer is the first place in the Bible where a king is called God's 'anointed' (Hebrew mashiach, the word behind 'Messiah'), years before Saul became Israel's first king. Luke does not quote her, but Mary's song (the Magnificat) follows the pattern of her prayer: God brings down the proud and mighty, lifts up the humble and fills the hungry (compare 1 Samuel 2:4-8 with Luke 1:51-53). Zechariah's 'horn of salvation for us in the house of His servant David' echoes Hannah's last line, 'He will exalt the horn of His anointed' ('horn' is a biblical picture of strength). It also recalls Psalm 18:2, where God is 'the horn of my salvation'. Christians have long read Hannah's hope as answered in Jesus, the Son of David.

title: The Eternal Davidic Throne & Sonship

ot.author: Nathan the Prophet
ot.context: The Davidic Covenant delivered to King David in Jerusalem.
ot.text: And when your days are fulfilled and you rest with your fathers, I will raise up your descendant after you, who will come from your own body, and I will establish his kingdom. He will build a house for My Name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever. I will be his Father, and he will be My son. When he does wrong, I will discipline him with the rod of men and with the blows of the sons of men. But My loving devotion will never be removed from him as I removed it from Saul, whom I moved out of your way. Your house and kingdom will endure forever before Me, and your throne will be established forever.” … And when your days are fulfilled and you go to be with your fathers, I will raise up your descendant after you, one of your own sons, and I will establish his kingdom. He will build a house for Me, and I will establish his throne forever. I will be his Father, and he will be My son. And I will never remove My loving devotion from him as I removed it from your predecessor. But I will set him over My house and My kingdom forever, and his throne will be established forever.”
ot.keyPhrase: I will be his Father, and he will be My son

nt.author: Luke / Author of Hebrews
nt.context: The angel Gabriel announces Jesus' birth to Mary in Nazareth; Hebrews applies God's promise about David's son to Christ.
nt.text: He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High. The Lord God will give Him the throne of His father David, and He will reign over the house of Jacob forever. His kingdom will never end!” … For to which of the angels did God ever say: “You are My Son; today I have become Your Father”? Or again: “I will be His Father, and He will be My Son”?
nt.keyPhrase: I will be His Father, and He will be My Son

bridge: Through the prophet Nathan, God promises David a descendant whose throne He will establish forever, and says, 'I will be his Father, and he will be My son.' In its first setting the promise concerned Solomon, who would build the temple, and it even allows that this son may do wrong and be disciplined. Because the promise says 'forever', later Jewish hope looked for a greater son of David, and the New Testament presents Jesus as that heir. Gabriel does not quote 2 Samuel 7, but his words to Mary clearly echo it: the Son of the Most High, the throne of His father David, a kingdom that will never end. Hebrews 1:5 then quotes the promise word for word and applies it to Christ.

title: The Virgin Birth & Sign of Immanuel

ot.author: Isaiah
ot.context: A sign given to King Ahaz and the house of David when Aram (Syria) and Israel (Ephraim) marched on Jerusalem, the so-called Syro-Ephraimite crisis.
ot.text: Therefore the Lord Himself will give you a sign: Behold, the virgin will be with child and will give birth to a son, and will call Him Immanuel.
ot.keyPhrase: the virgin will be with child and will give birth to a son, and will call Him Immanuel

nt.author: Matthew
nt.context: After the angel tells Joseph that Mary's child is from the Holy Spirit, Matthew links the birth to Isaiah's sign.
nt.text: All this took place to fulfill what the Lord had said through the prophet: “Behold, the virgin will be with child and will give birth to a son, and they will call Him Immanuel” (which means, “God with us”).
nt.keyPhrase: the virgin will be with child and will give birth to a son, and they will call Him Immanuel

bridge: Isaiah gave this sign to King Ahaz and the 'house of David' (Isaiah 7:13) when two enemy kings threatened Jerusalem. It also spoke to that crisis: before the boy knew right from wrong, the land of those kings would be laid waste (Isaiah 7:16). Matthew quotes the verse as fulfilled in the birth of Jesus to Mary, who was with child 'through the Holy Spirit' before she and Joseph came together (Matthew 1:18). Isaiah's Hebrew word, almah, means a young woman of marriageable age; the Greek translation Matthew follows says 'virgin'. Matthew presents Jesus as the sign's fullest meaning: Immanuel, 'God with us'.

title: Unto Us a Child is Born, Prince of Peace

ot.author: Isaiah
ot.context: Isaiah's prophecy of light after darkness: a royal child born to reign on David's throne with justice and peace.
ot.text: For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given, and the government will be upon His shoulders. And He will be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace. Of the increase of His government and peace there will be no end. He will reign on the throne of David and over his kingdom, to establish and sustain it with justice and righteousness from that time and forevermore. The zeal of the LORD of Hosts will accomplish this.
ot.keyPhrase: He will reign on the throne of David and over his kingdom

nt.author: Luke
nt.context: Gabriel promises Mary that her son will have David's throne and an endless kingdom; an angel announces His birth to the shepherds near Bethlehem.
nt.text: He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High. The Lord God will give Him the throne of His father David, and He will reign over the house of Jacob forever. His kingdom will never end!” … Today in the city of David a Savior has been born to you. He is Christ the Lord!
nt.keyPhrase: The Lord God will give Him the throne of His father David

bridge: Isaiah announces a royal child: 'For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given.' The two lines are Hebrew parallelism (one idea said twice in different words), so both describe the same birth of a king who will 'reign on the throne of David' in endless peace. No New Testament writer quotes these verses, but Luke's birth story echoes them: Gabriel says God will give Jesus 'the throne of His father David' and that 'His kingdom will never end' (Luke 1:32-33), and the angel tells the shepherds that a Savior is born 'in the city of David'. Christians later read 'a son is given' and the title 'Mighty God' in the light of the Incarnation (God the Son becoming human in Jesus); that is a theological reading of the passage, not something the parallel lines state by themselves.

title: The Shoot from the Stem of Jesse

ot.author: Isaiah
ot.context: Isaiah's picture of Jesse's family tree cut down to a stump, with a new shoot springing up from it.
ot.text: Then a shoot will spring up from the stump of Jesse, and a Branch from his roots will bear fruit. The Spirit of the LORD will rest on Him— the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and strength, the Spirit of knowledge and fear of the LORD. … On that day the Root of Jesse will stand as a banner for the peoples. The nations will seek Him, and His place of rest will be glorious.
ot.keyPhrase: the Root of Jesse will stand as a banner for the peoples

nt.author: Paul / Matthew
nt.context: Paul quotes Isaiah 11:10 to show that Christ's mission includes the Gentiles; at Jesus' baptism the Spirit of God descends and rests on Him.
nt.text: And once more, Isaiah says: “The Root of Jesse will appear, One who will arise to rule over the Gentiles; in Him the Gentiles will put their hope.” … As soon as Jesus was baptized, He went up out of the water. Suddenly the heavens were opened, and He saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and resting on Him.
nt.keyPhrase: The Root of Jesse will appear, One who will arise to rule over the Gentiles

bridge: Isaiah pictures the family of Jesse, David's father, as a tree cut down to a stump. From that stump a shoot springs up: a new ruler on whom 'The Spirit of the LORD will rest'. Many read the image as hope that David's royal line, though cut down, would grow again. Paul quotes Isaiah 11:10 in its ancient Greek form (Romans 15:12) to show that this Root of Jesse brings hope to the Gentiles. Many also hear an echo of 11:2 at Jesus' baptism, when the Spirit comes down and rests on Him (Matthew 3:16), though Matthew does not cite Isaiah there.

title: Born in Bethlehem Ephrathah

ot.author: Micah
ot.context: With Jerusalem under siege (Micah 5:1), the prophet looks to small Bethlehem, from which a ruler over Israel will come.
ot.text: But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, who are small among the clans of Judah, out of you will come forth for Me One to be ruler over Israel— One whose origins are of old, from the days of eternity.
ot.keyPhrase: But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, who are small among the clans of Judah, out of you will come forth

nt.author: Matthew / John
nt.context: When Herod asks where the Christ is to be born, the chief priests and scribes quote Micah; in John 7:42 the crowd recalls the same expectation.
nt.text: After Jesus was born in Bethlehem in Judea, during the time of King Herod, Magi from the east arrived in Jerusalem, asking, “Where is the One who has been born King of the Jews? We saw His star in the east and have come to worship Him.” When King Herod heard this, he was disturbed, and all Jerusalem with him. And when he had assembled all the chief priests and scribes of the people, he asked them where the Christ was to be born. “In Bethlehem in Judea,” they replied, “for this is what the prophet has written: ‘But you, Bethlehem, in the land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah, for out of you will come a ruler who will be the shepherd of My people Israel.’” … Doesn’t the Scripture say that the Christ will come from the line of David and from Bethlehem, the village where David lived?”
nt.keyPhrase: But you, Bethlehem, in the land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah

bridge: Micah, prophesying in the 700s BC, says that from Bethlehem Ephrathah, 'small among the clans of Judah', will come a ruler over Israel, 'One whose origins are of old, from the days of eternity.' When Herod asks where the Christ is to be born, the chief priests and scribes answer 'In Bethlehem in Judea' and quote this verse (Matthew 2:5-6). Their wording is freer: Bethlehem is 'by no means least', and the ruler 'will be the shepherd of My people Israel', words that echo God's promise to David (2 Samuel 5:2). John 7:42 shows the crowds shared this hope: the Christ would come 'from the line of David and from Bethlehem'. Luke tells how Joseph, of David's line, came to Bethlehem for a census (Luke 2:4-5).

title: Weeping in Ramah for the Slain Children

ot.author: Jeremiah
ot.context: Rachel, one of Israel's ancestral mothers, pictured weeping at Ramah, north of Jerusalem, as her descendants are taken into exile.
ot.text: This is what the LORD says: “A voice is heard in Ramah, mourning and great weeping, Rachel weeping for her children, and refusing to be comforted, because they are no more.”
ot.keyPhrase: Rachel weeping for her children, and refusing to be comforted, because they are no more

nt.author: Matthew
nt.context: King Herod ordering the massacre of male infants in Bethlehem and its surrounding districts.
nt.text: When Herod saw that he had been outwitted by the Magi, he was filled with rage. Sending orders, he put to death all the boys in Bethlehem and its vicinity who were two years old and under, according to the time he had learned from the Magi. Then what was spoken through the prophet Jeremiah was fulfilled: “A voice is heard in Ramah, weeping and great mourning, Rachel weeping for her children, and refusing to be comforted, because they are no more.”
nt.keyPhrase: Rachel weeping for her children, and refusing to be comforted, because they are no more

bridge: Matthew quotes Jeremiah 31:15 after Herod kills the boys of Bethlehem. In Jeremiah, Rachel (Jacob's wife and an ancestral mother of Israel) weeps at Ramah for descendants taken into exile; Ramah, north of Jerusalem, was where captives were gathered for Babylon (Jeremiah 40:1). Bethlehem lies south of Jerusalem, about 10 miles (16 km) from Ramah, and Genesis 35:19 places Rachel's grave on the way to Bethlehem. In Jeremiah her grief is followed at once by God's promise, 'your children will return to their own land' (Jeremiah 31:17), and later by a new covenant (Jeremiah 31:31). Many read Matthew as seeing that pattern repeat at the start of Jesus' life: bitter grief, then God's rescue.

title: Flight & Return: 'Out of Egypt I Called My Son'

ot.author: Hosea
ot.context: Recalling God's fatherly love for Israel in delivering the nation out of Egyptian bondage.
ot.text: When Israel was a child, I loved him, and out of Egypt I called My son.
ot.keyPhrase: out of Egypt I called My son

nt.author: Matthew
nt.context: Joseph taking Mary and Jesus to Egypt until Herod's death, then returning to the land of Israel.
nt.text: So he got up, took the Child and His mother by night, and withdrew to Egypt, where he stayed until the death of Herod. This fulfilled what the Lord had spoken through the prophet: “Out of Egypt I called My Son.”
nt.keyPhrase: Out of Egypt I called My Son

bridge: Classic biblical typology: Israel was God's corporate son called out of Egypt (Exod 4:22), and Jesus—the true, faithful Son—recapitulates Israel's history from Egypt through the waters of baptism into the wilderness.

title: The Messenger Preparing the Lord's Highway

ot.author: Isaiah & Malachi
ot.context: Closing words of the Hebrew prophets promising a forerunner before the Lord comes to His temple.
ot.text: A voice of one calling: “Prepare the way for the LORD in the wilderness; make a straight highway for our God in the desert. … “Behold, I will send My messenger, who will prepare the way before Me. Then the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to His temple—the Messenger of the covenant, in whom you delight—see, He is coming,” says the LORD of Hosts.
ot.keyPhrase: Prepare the way for the LORD in the wilderness

nt.author: Mark / Matthew
nt.context: John the Baptist emerging in the Judean wilderness calling the nation to repentance.
nt.text: As it is written in Isaiah the prophet: “Behold, I will send My messenger ahead of You, who will prepare Your way.” “A voice of one calling in the wilderness, ‘Prepare the way for the Lord, make straight paths for Him.’” John the Baptist appeared in the wilderness, preaching a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins. … This is the one about whom it is written: ‘Behold, I will send My messenger ahead of You, who will prepare Your way before You.’
nt.keyPhrase: Prepare the way for the Lord, make straight paths for Him

bridge: Notice the divinity implied in the cross-reference: in Isaiah 40:3 and Malachi 3:1, the highway is prepared for Yahweh Himself; in the Gospels, John prepares that road for Jesus.

title: Daniel's Seventy Weeks: The Anointed One & the Desolation

ot.author: Daniel (via the angel Gabriel)
ot.context: Gabriel tells Daniel of 'seventy weeks' for Jerusalem: an anointed one will come and be cut off, and the city and sanctuary will be destroyed.
ot.text: Seventy weeks are decreed for your people and your holy city to stop their transgression, to put an end to sin, to make atonement for iniquity, to bring in everlasting righteousness, to seal up vision and prophecy, and to anoint the Most Holy Place. Know and understand this: From the issuance of the decree to restore and rebuild Jerusalem, until the Messiah, the Prince, there will be seven weeks and sixty-two weeks. It will be rebuilt with streets and a trench, but in times of distress. Then after the sixty-two weeks the Messiah will be cut off and will have nothing. Then the people of the prince who is to come will destroy the city and the sanctuary. The end will come like a flood, and until the end there will be war; desolations have been decreed. And he will confirm a covenant with many for one week, but in the middle of the week he will put an end to sacrifice and offering. And on the wing of the temple will come the abomination that causes desolation, until the decreed destruction is poured out upon him.”
ot.keyPhrase: the abomination that causes desolation

nt.author: Matthew / Mark / Luke
nt.context: Jesus warns of 'the abomination of desolation' spoken of by Daniel, announces that 'The time is fulfilled', and foretells Jerusalem's fall.
nt.text: So when you see standing in the holy place ‘the abomination of desolation,’ described by the prophet Daniel (let the reader understand), … “The time is fulfilled,” He said, “and the kingdom of God is near. Repent and believe in the gospel!” … For the days will come upon you when your enemies will barricade you and surround you and hem you in on every side. They will level you to the ground—you and the children within your walls. They will not leave one stone on another, because you did not recognize the time of your visitation from God.”
nt.keyPhrase: the abomination of desolation

bridge: Daniel 9 speaks of 'seventy weeks' (seventy sevens, usually taken as 490 years): an anointed one, 'the Messiah, the Prince', comes and is later 'cut off', and the city and sanctuary are destroyed. Many Christians count 69 weeks (483 years) from a Persian decree and arrive near Jesus' time, but the result depends on which decree and which length of year one chooses. Many scholars read the passage as about the 2nd century BC, when a Greek king defiled the temple, and the Hebrew can also mean simply an anointed one, a prince. The New Testament never uses the timeline; Mark 1:15 and Luke 19:43-44 share only the ideas of an appointed time and the city's fall. Its clear use of the passage is Jesus' warning about 'the abomination of desolation', a sacrilege in the temple (Matthew 24:15), drawing on Daniel 9:27 and similar verses.

title: Great Light Dawning in Galilee of the Gentiles

ot.author: Isaiah
ot.context: Promise that the northern tribes of Zebulun and Naphtali, first humbled by Assyria, will see glory.
ot.text: Nevertheless, there will be no more gloom for those in distress. In the past He humbled the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, but in the future He will honor the Way of the Sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations: The people walking in darkness have seen a great light; on those living in the land of the shadow of death, a light has dawned.
ot.keyPhrase: The people walking in darkness have seen a great light

nt.author: Matthew
nt.context: Jesus moving from Nazareth to Capernaum on the border of Zebulun and Naphtali.
nt.text: When Jesus heard that John had been imprisoned, He withdrew to Galilee. Leaving Nazareth, He went and lived in Capernaum, which is by the sea in the region of Zebulun and Naphtali, to fulfill what was spoken through the prophet Isaiah: “Land of Zebulun and land of Naphtali, the Way of the Sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles— the people living in darkness have seen a great light; on those living in the land of the shadow of death, a light has dawned.”
nt.keyPhrase: the people living in darkness have seen a great light

bridge: Rather than launching His ministry in prestigious Judea, Jesus made Capernaum in Galilee His headquarters—bringing divine light to the exact region first plunged into Assyrian darkness.

title: Anointed to Preach Good News & Proclaim the Lord's Favor

ot.author: Isaiah
ot.context: A speaker anointed by the Spirit announces good news to the poor, liberty to captives and the year of the LORD's favor.
ot.text: The Spirit of the Lord GOD is on Me, because the LORD has anointed Me to preach good news to the poor. He has sent Me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives and freedom to the prisoners, to proclaim the year of the LORD’s favor and the day of our God’s vengeance, to comfort all who mourn,
ot.keyPhrase: the LORD has anointed Me to preach good news to the poor

nt.author: Luke
nt.context: Jesus reads from the scroll of Isaiah in the synagogue at Nazareth.
nt.text: Then Jesus came to Nazareth, where He had been brought up. As was His custom, He entered the synagogue on the Sabbath. And when He stood up to read, the scroll of the prophet Isaiah was handed to Him. Unrolling it, He found the place where it was written: “The Spirit of the Lord is on Me, because He has anointed Me to preach good news to the poor. He has sent Me to proclaim liberty to the captives and recovery of sight to the blind, to release the oppressed, to proclaim the year of the Lord’s favor.” Then He rolled up the scroll, returned it to the attendant, and sat down. The eyes of everyone in the synagogue were fixed on Him, and He began by saying, “Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing.”
nt.keyPhrase: He has anointed Me to preach good news to the poor

bridge: In the synagogue at Nazareth, Jesus reads Isaiah 61:1-2 and then says, 'Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing.' Luke's wording follows the ancient Greek translation of Isaiah and adds a line drawn from Isaiah 58:6 ('to set the oppressed free'). Isaiah's 'proclaim liberty' recalls the Jubilee, the fiftieth year when liberty was proclaimed and each family returned to its land (Leviticus 25:10). The reading ends with 'the year of the Lord’s favor', just before Isaiah's next words, 'the day of our God’s vengeance'. Many Christians see this stopping point as dividing Christ's first coming in grace from His return in judgment, but Luke gives no reason for it.

title: The Prophet Like Unto Moses

ot.author: Moses
ot.context: Moses' farewell address promising a future Prophet-Mediator who speaks God's very words.
ot.text: The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers. You must listen to him. This is what you asked of the LORD your God at Horeb on the day of the assembly, when you said, “Let us not hear the voice of the LORD our God or see this great fire anymore, so that we will not die!” Then the LORD said to me, “They have spoken well. I will raise up for them a prophet like you from among their brothers. I will put My words in his mouth, and he will tell them everything I command him. And I will hold accountable anyone who does not listen to My words that the prophet speaks in My name.
ot.keyPhrase: The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers

nt.author: Peter / John
nt.context: Peter preaching at Solomon's Portico in the Jerusalem Temple.
nt.text: For Moses said, ‘The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers. You must listen to Him in everything He tells you. Everyone who does not listen to Him will be completely cut off from among his people.’ … When the people saw the sign that Jesus had performed, they began to say, “Truly this is the Prophet who is to come into the world.”
nt.keyPhrase: The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers

bridge: Like Moses, Jesus was spared from a tyrant's infanticide at birth, called out of Egypt, fasted 40 days, fed multitudes with bread in the wilderness, ascended a mountain to teach God's law, and mediated a covenant.

title: Miracles of Sight to the Blind & Hearing to the Deaf

ot.author: Isaiah
ot.context: Isaiah's vision of the desert in bloom and the redeemed returning to Zion when God comes to save His people.
ot.text: Say to those with anxious hearts: “Be strong, do not fear! Behold, your God will come with vengeance. With divine retribution He will come to save you.” Then the eyes of the blind will be opened and the ears of the deaf unstopped. Then the lame will leap like a deer and the mute tongue will shout for joy. For waters will gush forth in the wilderness, and streams in the desert.
ot.keyPhrase: Then the eyes of the blind will be opened and the ears of the deaf unstopped

nt.author: Matthew / Mark
nt.context: Jesus answers the messengers John the Baptist sent from prison, and a crowd marvels when He heals a deaf man who could hardly speak.
nt.text: Jesus replied, “Go back and report to John what you hear and see: The blind receive sight, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the good news is preached to the poor. … Some people brought to Him a man who was deaf and hardly able to speak, and they begged Jesus to place His hand on him. … The people were utterly astonished and said, “He has done all things well! He makes even the deaf hear and the mute speak!”
nt.keyPhrase: The blind receive sight, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear

bridge: Isaiah 35 pictures the day when God comes to save His people: 'Then the eyes of the blind will be opened and the ears of the deaf unstopped.' When John the Baptist sends from prison to ask whether Jesus is 'the One who was to come' (Matthew 11:3), Jesus answers by pointing to these very signs: the blind see, the lame walk, the deaf hear. He does not quote Isaiah, but the echo is clear, and His list also recalls the good news for the poor promised in Isaiah 61:1. In Mark 7:32, the deaf man 'hardly able to speak' is described with a rare Greek word that the Greek Old Testament uses only in Isaiah 35:6. Christians read these healings as signs that the salvation God promised had come in Jesus.

title: Speaking Hidden Kingdom Truths in Parables

ot.author: Asaph
ot.context: A teaching psalm of Asaph that retells Israel's history, from the Exodus to King David, as lessons for the next generation.
ot.text: I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter things hidden from the beginning,
ot.keyPhrase: I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter things hidden

nt.author: Matthew
nt.context: Jesus teaching the crowds by the Sea of Galilee in parables of the Kingdom.
nt.text: Jesus spoke all these things to the crowds in parables. He did not tell them anything without using a parable. So was fulfilled what was spoken through the prophet: “I will open My mouth in parables; I will utter things hidden since the foundation of the world.”
nt.keyPhrase: I will open My mouth in parables; I will utter things hidden

bridge: Psalm 78 opens with Asaph promising to speak in parables and to utter 'things hidden from the beginning'. He means the lessons of Israel's history, which the fathers passed on so that their children would trust God (Psalm 78:3-7). Matthew notes that Jesus taught the crowds only in parables, and says this 'fulfilled what was spoken through the prophet'. On its own terms the psalm is not a prediction, so many read Matthew as seeing a pattern rather than a forecast: as Asaph drew hidden lessons from Israel's story, Jesus brings to light things 'hidden since the foundation of the world'.

title: Gentle Servant Who Will Not Break a Bruised Reed

ot.author: Isaiah
ot.context: The First Servant Song introducing God's gentle, Spirit-filled Servant bringing justice to the nations.
ot.text: “Here is My Servant, whom I uphold, My Chosen One, in whom My soul delights. I will put My Spirit on Him, and He will bring justice to the nations. He will not cry out or raise His voice, nor make His voice heard in the streets. A bruised reed He will not break and a smoldering wick He will not extinguish; He will faithfully bring forth justice. He will not grow weak or discouraged before He has established justice on the earth. In His law the islands will put their hope.”
ot.keyPhrase: A bruised reed He will not break and a smoldering wick He will not extinguish

nt.author: Matthew
nt.context: Jesus quietly healing the sick while avoiding political confrontation with the Pharisees.
nt.text: Aware of this, Jesus withdrew from that place. Large crowds followed Him, and He healed them all, warning them not to make Him known. This was to fulfill what was spoken through the prophet Isaiah: “Here is My Servant, whom I have chosen, My beloved, in whom My soul delights. I will put My Spirit on Him, and He will proclaim justice to the nations. He will not quarrel or cry out; no one will hear His voice in the streets. A bruised reed He will not break, and a smoldering wick He will not extinguish, till He leads justice to victory. In His name the nations will put their hope.”
nt.keyPhrase: A bruised reed He will not break, and a smoldering wick He will not extinguish

bridge: Unlike political zealots who crushed the weak in pursuit of power, Jesus tended to 'bruised reeds' and 'smoldering wicks'—the broken, outcast, and exhausted.

title: The Commander of the Lord's Army

ot.author: Joshua
ot.context: Near Jericho, a man with a drawn sword says he has come as Commander of the LORD's army and orders Joshua to take off his sandals, for the place is holy.
ot.text: Now when Joshua was near Jericho, he looked up and saw a man standing in front of him with a drawn sword in His hand. Joshua approached Him and asked, “Are You for us or for our enemies?” “Neither,” He replied. “I have now come as Commander of the LORD’s army.” Then Joshua fell facedown in reverence and asked Him, “What does my Lord have to say to His servant?” The Commander of the LORD’s army replied, “Take off your sandals, for the place where you are standing is holy.” And Joshua did so.
ot.keyPhrase: I have now come as Commander of the LORD’s army

nt.author: John
nt.context: John sees heaven open and a rider called Faithful and True, the Word of God, who judges and wages war with the armies of heaven following Him.
nt.text: Then I saw heaven standing open, and there before me was a white horse. And its rider is called Faithful and True. With righteousness He judges and wages war. He has eyes like blazing fire, and many royal crowns on His head. He has a name written on Him that only He Himself knows. He is dressed in a robe dipped in blood, and His name is The Word of God. The armies of heaven, dressed in fine linen, white and pure, follow Him on white horses.
nt.keyPhrase: The armies of heaven, dressed in fine linen, white and pure, follow Him

bridge: Near Jericho, Joshua meets a man with a drawn sword who says he has come 'as Commander of the LORD’s army'. Joshua falls facedown before him, a gesture also made to kings (2 Samuel 14:4), and is told to take off his sandals because the place is holy, as Moses was at the burning bush (Exodus 3:5). Because of that echo, many Christians have read this figure as a Christophany (an appearance of the Son of God before His birth as a man). The New Testament never mentions this scene or says who the Commander is. Revelation 19:11-14 is only a loose parallel: the rider called Faithful and True, whose name is 'The Word of God', leads 'the armies of heaven', but the two passages share a picture, not wording.

title: Manna from Heaven & Water from the Struck Rock

ot.author: Moses / Asaph
ot.context: God sustaining Israel in the wilderness with daily bread from heaven and water from the rock at Horeb; Psalm 78 later recalls the manna.
ot.text: Then the LORD said to Moses, “Behold, I will rain down bread from heaven for you. Each day the people are to go out and gather enough for that day. In this way I will test whether or not they will follow My instructions. … When the Israelites saw it, they asked one another, “What is it?” For they did not know what it was. So Moses told them, “It is the bread that the LORD has given you to eat. … Behold, I will stand there before you by the rock at Horeb. And when you strike the rock, water will come out of it for the people to drink.” So Moses did this in the sight of the elders of Israel. … He rained down manna for them to eat; He gave them grain from heaven.
ot.keyPhrase: I will rain down bread from heaven for you

nt.author: John / Paul
nt.context: Jesus declaring 'I am the bread of life' and Paul identifying the wilderness Rock as Christ.
nt.text: Our fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, as it is written: ‘He gave them bread from heaven to eat.’” Jesus said to them, “Truly, truly, I tell you, it was not Moses who gave you the bread from heaven, but it is My Father who gives you the true bread from heaven. For the bread of God is He who comes down from heaven and gives life to the world.” “Sir,” they said, “give us this bread at all times.” Jesus answered, “I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to Me will never hunger, and whoever believes in Me will never thirst. … They all ate the same spiritual food and drank the same spiritual drink; for they drank from the spiritual rock that accompanied them, and that rock was Christ.
nt.keyPhrase: it is My Father who gives you the true bread from heaven

bridge: In John 6 the crowd recalls the manna with a line of Scripture, 'He gave them bread from heaven to eat', which draws on Exodus 16:4, 15 and Psalm 78:24. Jesus answers that it is His Father who gives 'the true bread from heaven', and says, 'I am the bread of life.' Paul calls Israel's wilderness food and drink 'spiritual' and says of the rock that gave water, 'that rock was Christ.' So the New Testament itself reads both gifts as typology (earlier events that foreshadow Christ). Some Christians also see the striking of the rock as a picture of Christ's suffering, but Paul does not say this.

title: The Bronze Serpent Lifted Up in the Wilderness

ot.author: Moses
ot.context: God commands Moses to mount a bronze serpent on a pole so anyone bitten who looks in faith lives.
ot.text: Then the LORD said to Moses, “Make a fiery serpent and mount it on a pole. When anyone who is bitten looks at it, he will live.” So Moses made a bronze snake and mounted it on a pole. If anyone who was bitten looked at the bronze snake, he would live.
ot.keyPhrase: Moses made a bronze snake and mounted it on a pole

nt.author: John (Words of Jesus to Nicodemus)
nt.context: Jesus explaining the necessity of the Cross to Nicodemus just before John 3:16.
nt.text: Just as Moses lifted up the snake in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up, that everyone who believes in Him may have eternal life.
nt.keyPhrase: Just as Moses lifted up the snake in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up

bridge: When venomous snakes were killing the Israelites, God told Moses to set a bronze snake on a pole, and anyone bitten who looked at it lived. Jesus Himself draws the comparison: as Moses lifted up the snake, 'so the Son of Man must be lifted up, that everyone who believes in Him may have eternal life.' Why a snake? Scripture does not say, but many Christians link it with Paul's words that God made Christ 'to be sin on our behalf' (2 Corinthians 5:21): the image of what was killing the people became the means of their healing. Some later interpreters also took bronze as a symbol of judgment, but that is a symbolic reading, not something the Bible states.

title: Miracles of Elisha: Multiplying Loaves & Cleansing Naaman

ot.author: Anonymous (later Jewish tradition: Jeremiah)
ot.context: Elisha feeds a hundred men with twenty barley loaves and some is left over; later Naaman, a Syrian army commander, washes in the Jordan at Elisha's word and is cleansed of leprosy.
ot.text: Now a man from Baal-shalishah came to the man of God with a sack of twenty loaves of barley bread from the first ripe grain. “Give it to the people to eat,” said Elisha. But his servant asked, “How am I to set twenty loaves before a hundred men?” “Give it to the people to eat,” said Elisha, “for this is what the LORD says: ‘They will eat and have some left over.’” So he set it before them, and they ate and had some left over, according to the word of the LORD. … So Naaman went down and dipped himself in the Jordan seven times, according to the word of the man of God, and his flesh was restored and became like that of a little child, and he was clean.
ot.keyPhrase: twenty loaves of barley bread

nt.author: John / Luke
nt.context: John: Jesus feeds about five thousand men with five barley loaves, and twelve baskets of pieces are left. Luke: at Nazareth, Jesus recalls that in Elisha's time only Naaman the Syrian was cleansed.
nt.text: “Here is a boy with five barley loaves and two small fish. But what difference will these make among so many?” “Have the people sit down,” Jesus said. Now there was plenty of grass in that place, so the men sat down, about five thousand of them. Then Jesus took the loaves and the fish, gave thanks, and distributed to those who were seated as much as they wanted. And when everyone was full, He said to His disciples, “Gather the pieces that are left over, so that nothing will be wasted.” So they collected them and filled twelve baskets with the pieces of the five barley loaves left over by those who had eaten. … And there were many lepers in Israel in the time of Elisha the prophet. Yet not one of them was cleansed—only Naaman the Syrian.”
nt.keyPhrase: a boy with five barley loaves and two small fish

bridge: Elisha once fed a hundred men with twenty barley loaves; his servant objected that it was too little, yet 'they ate and had some left over' (2 Kings 4:44). Only John's Gospel says the loaves Jesus used were barley, and the pattern repeats: a helper doubts, everyone eats, and twelve baskets of pieces are left. John never names Elisha, but many readers see a deliberate echo, with Jesus doing far more than the prophet did. Some go further: Jesus called John the Baptist 'the Elijah who was to come' (Matthew 11:14), and as Elisha followed Elijah, Jesus followed John. Elisha is named in Luke 4:27, where Jesus recalls Naaman's cleansing as God's mercy to a foreigner, not as a picture of His own healings.

title: Triumphal Entry on a Humble Donkey

ot.author: Zechariah
ot.context: A prophecy from after the exile, calling Jerusalem to rejoice at her righteous, humble King.
ot.text: Rejoice greatly, O Daughter of Zion! Shout in triumph, O Daughter of Jerusalem! See, your King comes to you, righteous and victorious, humble and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey.
ot.keyPhrase: humble and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey

nt.author: Matthew / John
nt.context: Jesus rides into Jerusalem on a young donkey as the crowds spread branches and shout Hosanna.
nt.text: This took place to fulfill what was spoken through the prophet: “Say to the Daughter of Zion, ‘See, your King comes to you, gentle and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey.’” … Finding a young donkey, Jesus sat on it, as it is written: “Do not be afraid, O Daughter of Zion. See, your King is coming, seated on the colt of a donkey.”
nt.keyPhrase: gentle and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey

bridge: Zechariah's King comes to Jerusalem 'humble and riding on a donkey', and the next verse promises that the chariot and the horse will be cut off and that He 'will proclaim peace to the nations' (Zechariah 9:10). Israel's kings did not always ride war horses: Solomon rode to his anointing on King David's own mule (1 Kings 1:33). Jesus sends His disciples to bring a donkey and her colt (Matthew 21:2), and Matthew and John both present His entry as the fulfillment of these words. Many read the scene as Jesus showing what kind of King He is: one who comes in humility and peace, not as a conqueror on a war horse.

title: Zeal for the Father's House & Children's Praise in the Temple

ot.author: David
ot.context: David's passion for the purity of God's sanctuary and praise rising from infants.
ot.text: because zeal for Your house has consumed me, and the insults of those who insult You have fallen on me. … From the mouths of children and infants You have ordained praise on account of Your adversaries, to silence the enemy and avenger.
ot.keyPhrase: zeal for Your house has consumed me

nt.author: John / Matthew
nt.context: Jesus cleansing the Temple courts and defending the children crying 'Hosanna to the Son of David!'
nt.text: His disciples remembered that it is written: “Zeal for Your house will consume Me.” … But the chief priests and scribes were indignant when they saw the wonders He performed and the children shouting in the temple courts, “Hosanna to the Son of David!” “Do You hear what these children are saying?” they asked. “Yes,” Jesus answered. “Have you never read: ‘From the mouths of children and infants You have ordained praise’?”
nt.keyPhrase: Zeal for Your house will consume Me

bridge: When the chief priests objected to children praising Jesus as the Son of David in the Temple courts, Jesus quoted Psalm 8:2—where the praise is directed to Yahweh—applying it directly to Himself.

title: Betrayed by a Trusted Friend Who Shared Bread

ot.author: David
ot.context: David grieves that a trusted friend who shared his bread has turned against him; tradition often links these psalms with Ahithophel, though neither names him.
ot.text: Even my close friend whom I trusted, the one who shared my bread, has lifted up his heel against me. … For it is not an enemy who insults me; that I could endure. It is not a foe who rises against me; from him I could hide. But it is you, a man like myself, my companion and close friend. We shared sweet fellowship together; we walked with the crowd into the house of God.
ot.keyPhrase: the one who shared my bread, has lifted up his heel against me

nt.author: John
nt.context: The Last Supper: Jesus handing the dipped morsel of bread to Judas Iscariot.
nt.text: I am not speaking about all of you; I know whom I have chosen. But this is to fulfill the Scripture: ‘The one who shares My bread has lifted up his heel against Me.’ … Jesus answered, “It is the one to whom I give this morsel after I have dipped it.” Then He dipped the morsel and gave it to Judas son of Simon Iscariot.
nt.keyPhrase: The one who shares My bread has lifted up his heel against Me

bridge: At the Last Supper Jesus quotes Psalm 41:9 as Scripture to be fulfilled: 'The one who shares My bread has lifted up his heel against Me.' In the psalm the traitor is 'my close friend whom I trusted', and lifting the heel pictures turning against someone. Jesus then gives the dipped morsel to Judas. Psalm 55:12-14 is not quoted in the New Testament, but it voices the same pain of betrayal by a close friend. Many readers link both psalms with Ahithophel, David's counselor who joined Absalom's conspiracy and later hanged himself (2 Samuel 15:12, 31; 17:23), as Judas did (Matthew 27:5), though neither psalm names him.

title: Sold for Thirty Pieces of Silver & Thrown to the Potter

ot.author: Zechariah
ot.context: Acting as shepherd of a flock marked for slaughter, the prophet is paid thirty pieces of silver, the sum the Law set for a slave gored by an ox (Exodus 21:32), and throws it to the potter in the house of the LORD.
ot.text: Then I told them, “If it seems right to you, give me my wages; but if not, keep them.” So they weighed out my wages, thirty pieces of silver. And the LORD said to me, “Throw it to the potter”—this magnificent price at which they valued me. So I took the thirty pieces of silver and threw them to the potter in the house of the LORD.
ot.keyPhrase: I took the thirty pieces of silver and threw them to the potter

nt.author: Matthew
nt.context: Judas throws the thirty pieces of silver into the temple and the priests use them to buy the potter's field; Matthew says this fulfilled words spoken through Jeremiah.
nt.text: and asked, “What are you willing to give me if I hand Him over to you?” And they set out for him thirty pieces of silver. … When Judas, who had betrayed Him, saw that Jesus was condemned, he was filled with remorse and returned the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders. “I have sinned by betraying innocent blood,” he said. “What is that to us?” they replied. “You bear the responsibility.” So Judas threw the silver into the temple and left. Then he went away and hanged himself. The chief priests picked up the pieces of silver and said, “It is unlawful to put this into the treasury, since it is blood money.” After conferring together, they used the money to buy the potter’s field as a burial place for foreigners. That is why it has been called the Field of Blood to this day. Then what was spoken through Jeremiah the prophet was fulfilled: “They took the thirty pieces of silver, the price set on Him by the people of Israel, and they gave them for the potter’s field, as the Lord had commanded me.”
nt.keyPhrase: They took the thirty pieces of silver, the price set on Him

bridge: In Zechariah 11 the prophet, acting as shepherd of a doomed flock, is paid off with thirty pieces of silver, 'this magnificent price at which they valued me', and the LORD tells him to throw it to the potter in His house. Matthew finds the same details in the story of Judas: thirty pieces of silver paid by the chief priests (Matthew 26:15), thrown into the temple, then used to buy the potter's field. Matthew says this fulfilled 'what was spoken through Jeremiah the prophet', yet the wording comes chiefly from Zechariah. This is usually explained as a combined citation (words from more than one prophet given under one name): Jeremiah, too, went to a potter's house, bought a potter's clay jar and bought a field (Jeremiah 18:2-3; 19:1; 32:9).

title: Strike the Shepherd and the Sheep Will Be Scattered

ot.author: Zechariah
ot.context: Prophetic command for the sword to strike the Lord's Shepherd, scattering the flock.
ot.text: Awake, O sword, against My Shepherd, against the man who is My Companion, declares the LORD of Hosts. Strike the Shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered, and I will turn My hand against the little ones.
ot.keyPhrase: Strike the Shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered

nt.author: Matthew / Mark
nt.context: On the walk to Gethsemane, Jesus warns the disciples that they will all flee at His arrest.
nt.text: Then Jesus said to them, “This very night you will all fall away on account of Me. For it is written: ‘I will strike the Shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered.’ … But this has all happened so that the writings of the prophets would be fulfilled.” Then all the disciples deserted Him and fled. … Then Jesus said to them, “You will all fall away, for it is written: ‘I will strike the Shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered.’
nt.keyPhrase: I will strike the Shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered

bridge: Jesus quotes Zechariah 13:7 with 'it is written' and applies it to that night: His arrest and the disciples' flight. He turns the command 'Strike the Shepherd' into God's own act: 'I will strike the Shepherd.' Matthew then reports that 'all the disciples deserted Him and fled.' In Zechariah, God calls the Shepherd 'the man who is My Companion'; the Hebrew word means a companion or close associate, not an equal, though some Christians have seen in this closeness a hint of Christ's divine nature. The Gospels use the verse for the scattering of the disciples, and Jesus at once adds, 'after I have risen, I will go ahead of you into Galilee' (Matthew 26:32).

title: Silent as a Lamb Before Its Shearers

ot.author: Isaiah
ot.context: The Suffering Servant submitting willingly without self-defense.
ot.text: He was oppressed and afflicted, yet He did not open His mouth. He was led like a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before her shearers is silent, so He did not open His mouth.
ot.keyPhrase: as a sheep before her shearers is silent, so He did not open His mouth

nt.author: Luke / Matthew / Peter
nt.context: Jesus stays silent before the high priest Caiaphas, Herod Antipas and Pilate; later an Ethiopian official reads Isaiah 53:7-8 and Philip explains it as being about Jesus.
nt.text: The eunuch was reading this passage of Scripture: “He was led like a sheep to the slaughter, and as a lamb before the shearer is silent, so He did not open His mouth. In His humiliation He was deprived of justice. Who can recount His descendants? For His life was removed from the earth.” “Tell me,” said the eunuch, “who is the prophet talking about, himself or someone else?” Then Philip began with this very Scripture and told him the good news about Jesus. … But Jesus remained silent. Then the high priest said to Him, “I charge You under oath by the living God: Tell us if You are the Christ, the Son of God.” … And when He was accused by the chief priests and elders, He gave no answer. Then Pilate asked Him, “Do You not hear how many charges they are bringing against You?” But Jesus gave no answer, not even to a single charge, much to the governor’s amazement. … Herod questioned Jesus at great length, but He gave no answer. … When they heaped abuse on Him, He did not retaliate; when He suffered, He made no threats, but entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly.
nt.keyPhrase: as a lamb before the shearer is silent, so He did not open His mouth

bridge: Isaiah 53 describes the Servant of the LORD, often called the Suffering Servant, who suffers without protest: like a sheep before her shearers, 'He did not open His mouth.' The Gospels show Jesus silent in the same way before the high priest, before Herod and before Pilate, who was amazed that He gave no answer. They do not quote Isaiah at these points, though many readers hear an echo of it. Acts makes the link explicit: an Ethiopian official was reading this very passage, and Philip 'began with this very Scripture and told him the good news about Jesus.' Peter likewise holds up Jesus as an example: 'When they heaped abuse on Him, He did not retaliate'.

title: Beaten, Spat Upon & Flogged

ot.author: Isaiah
ot.context: In the third Servant Song (one of Isaiah's poems about the LORD's servant), the speaker offers his back to beatings and does not hide his face from spitting.
ot.text: I offered My back to those who struck Me, and My cheeks to those who tore out My beard. I did not hide My face from scorn and spittle.
ot.keyPhrase: I did not hide My face from scorn and spittle

nt.author: Matthew / Luke
nt.context: Jesus is spat on and struck at His hearing before the Jewish council, flogged on Pilate's orders and beaten by soldiers; earlier He tells the Twelve that this will fulfill what the prophets wrote.
nt.text: Then they spit in His face and struck Him. Others slapped Him … So Pilate released Barabbas to them. But he had Jesus flogged, and handed Him over to be crucified. … Then they spit on Him and took the staff and struck Him on the head repeatedly. … Then Jesus took the Twelve aside and said to them, “Look, we are going up to Jerusalem, and everything the prophets have written about the Son of Man will be fulfilled. He will be delivered over to the Gentiles and will be mocked and insulted and spit upon. They will flog Him and kill Him, and on the third day He will rise again.”
nt.keyPhrase: Then they spit in His face and struck Him

bridge: In Isaiah 50:6 the speaker, usually identified with the LORD's Servant (Isaiah 50:10), says, 'I offered My back to those who struck Me', and he did not hide his face from 'scorn and spittle'. Matthew records that Jesus was spat on and struck at His hearing before the Jewish council (the Sanhedrin), flogged on Pilate's orders, and spat on and beaten with a staff by Roman soldiers. Matthew does not quote Isaiah here. But Jesus had told the Twelve that 'everything the prophets have written about the Son of Man will be fulfilled': He would be 'spit upon' and flogged (Luke 18:31-33). Christians have long read Isaiah 50:6 as one of those writings, though the Gospels do not mention the beard Isaiah speaks of.

title: Pierced Hands and Feet & the Marks of the Nails

ot.author: David
ot.context: A lament of David: a sufferer surrounded by enemies cries out to God, and the psalm ends in praise for His rescue.
ot.text: For dogs surround me; a band of evil men encircles me; they have pierced my hands and feet.
ot.keyPhrase: they have pierced my hands and feet

nt.author: John / Luke
nt.context: The risen Jesus shows His hands and feet to the disciples and invites the doubting Thomas to touch His wounds.
nt.text: So the other disciples told him, “We have seen the Lord!” But he replied, “Unless I see the nail marks in His hands, and put my finger where the nails have been, and put my hand into His side, I will never believe.” Eight days later, His disciples were once again inside with the doors locked, and Thomas was with them. Jesus came and stood among them and said, “Peace be with you.” Then Jesus said to Thomas, “Put your finger here and look at My hands. Reach out your hand and put it into My side. Stop doubting and believe.” … Look at My hands and My feet. It is I Myself. Touch Me and see—for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see I have.” And when He had said this, He showed them His hands and feet.
nt.keyPhrase: the nail marks in His hands

bridge: Psalm 22 is a lament (a prayer from deep distress) in which a sufferer surrounded by enemies says 'they have pierced my hands and feet'. The Gospels quote other lines of this psalm at the cross (Matthew 27:46; John 19:24), but no New Testament writer quotes this verse. The risen Jesus shows His hands and feet to the disciples (Luke 24:39-40), and Thomas speaks of 'the nail marks in His hands', so Christians have long read the verse as a picture of the crucifixion. The wording is uncertain: the standard Hebrew text compares the attackers to a lion at this point, while the ancient Greek translation and a scroll fragment from Nahal Hever, near the Dead Sea, point to a verb whose exact meaning is debated.

title: Dividing Garments & Casting Lots for His Tunic

ot.author: David
ot.context: A sufferer surrounded by enemies sees them divide his garments and cast lots for his clothing; the two lines say one thing twice, as Hebrew poetry often does.
ot.text: They divide my garments among them and cast lots for my clothing.
ot.keyPhrase: They divide my garments among them and cast lots for my clothing

nt.author: John (Eyewitness at the Cross)
nt.context: The soldiers at the cross divide Jesus' garments into four shares, one each, then cast lots for His seamless tunic.
nt.text: When the soldiers had crucified Jesus, they divided His garments into four parts, one for each soldier, with the tunic remaining. It was seamless, woven in one piece from top to bottom. So they said to one another, “Let us not tear it. Instead, let us cast lots to see who will get it.” This was to fulfill the Scripture: “They divided My garments among them, and cast lots for My clothing.” So that is what the soldiers did.
nt.keyPhrase: They divided My garments among them, and cast lots for My clothing

bridge: Psalm 22:18 is Hebrew poetry, which often says one thing twice in different words; this is called parallelism. In the psalm, dividing the garments and casting lots for the clothing describe a single scene. John sees both lines happen separately at the cross: the soldiers divide Jesus' garments into four shares, then cast lots for His seamless tunic rather than tear it. He introduces the psalm with 'This was to fulfill the Scripture' and adds, 'So that is what the soldiers did.'

title: Pierced for Our Transgressions & Numbered with Transgressors

ot.author: Isaiah
ot.context: The heart of the fourth Servant Song: the Servant suffers for the sins of others, is counted among the transgressors, and intercedes for them.
ot.text: But He was pierced for our transgressions, He was crushed for our iniquities; the punishment that brought us peace was upon Him, and by His stripes we are healed. We all like sheep have gone astray, each one has turned to his own way; and the LORD has laid upon Him the iniquity of us all. … Therefore I will allot Him a portion with the great, and He will divide the spoils with the strong, because He has poured out His life unto death, and He was numbered with the transgressors. Yet He bore the sin of many and made intercession for the transgressors.
ot.keyPhrase: by His stripes we are healed

nt.author: Peter / Luke
nt.context: Jesus says the words 'numbered with the transgressors' must be fulfilled in Him; He is crucified between two criminals and prays 'Father, forgive them'; Peter applies Isaiah 53 to His death.
nt.text: He Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree, so that we might die to sin and live to righteousness. “By His stripes you are healed.” For “you were like sheep going astray,” but now you have returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls. … For I tell you that this Scripture must be fulfilled in Me: ‘And He was numbered with the transgressors.’ For what is written about Me is reaching its fulfillment.” … When they came to the place called The Skull, they crucified Him there, along with the criminals, one on His right and the other on His left. Then Jesus said, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.” And they divided up His garments by casting lots.
nt.keyPhrase: By His stripes you are healed

bridge: In the fourth Servant Song (a poem in Isaiah about the LORD's suffering servant), the Servant is 'pierced for our transgressions' and 'numbered with the transgressors', yet 'made intercession for the transgressors'. The New Testament applies particular lines of it to Jesus: Peter quotes 'By His stripes you are healed' and 'you were like sheep going astray' (1 Peter 2:24-25), drawing on Isaiah 53:5-6. On the night of His arrest Jesus Himself quotes 'And He was numbered with the transgressors', saying it 'must be fulfilled in Me' (Luke 22:37), and He is then crucified between two criminals. His prayer 'Father, forgive them' is often read as the Servant's intercession, though Luke does not cite Isaiah there.

title: Forsaken Cry & Mocked at the Cross ('Let God deliver Him')

ot.author: David
ot.context: The opening cry of Psalm 22 and the taunts of mockers who shake their heads.
ot.text: For the choirmaster. To the tune of “The Doe of the Dawn.” A Psalm of David. My God, my God, why have You forsaken me? Why are You so far from saving me, so far from my words of groaning? … All who see me mock me; they sneer and shake their heads: “He trusts in the LORD, let the LORD deliver him; let the LORD rescue him, since He delights in him.”
ot.keyPhrase: My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?

nt.author: Matthew
nt.context: Passersby shaking their heads, chief priests mocking, and Jesus crying out the opening line of Psalm 22.
nt.text: And those who passed by heaped abuse on Him, shaking their heads and saying, “You who are going to destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days, save Yourself! If You are the Son of God, come down from the cross!” In the same way, the chief priests, scribes, and elders mocked Him, saying, “He saved others, but He cannot save Himself. He is the King of Israel! Let Him come down now from the cross, and we will believe in Him. He trusts in God. Let God deliver Him now if He wants Him. For He said, ‘I am the Son of God.’” In the same way, even the robbers who were crucified with Him berated Him. From the sixth hour until the ninth hour darkness came over all the land. About the ninth hour Jesus cried out in a loud voice, “Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani?” which means, “My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?”
nt.keyPhrase: My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?

bridge: Jesus' cry 'Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani?' is the opening line of Psalm 22, and Matthew translates it for his readers. Matthew also describes the mockers in the psalm's terms: passers-by shake their heads (Psalm 22:7) and the leaders say, 'He trusts in God. Let God deliver Him' (compare Psalm 22:8). Many readers think that quoting a psalm's first line could call the whole psalm to mind, though this is debated. If so, the cry also points to the psalm's ending, where 'All the families of the nations will bow down before Him' (Psalm 22:27) and people proclaim 'all that He has done' (Psalm 22:31). Some Christians hear in this an echo of 'It is finished' (John 19:30), a devotional link the New Testament does not make.

title: Offered Gall and Sour Wine (Vinegar) for His Thirst

ot.author: David
ot.context: The righteous sufferer given bitter gall and sour vinegar in his parched agony.
ot.text: They poisoned my food with gall and gave me vinegar to quench my thirst.
ot.keyPhrase: They poisoned my food with gall and gave me vinegar to quench my thirst

nt.author: John
nt.context: Soldiers lifting a sponge soaked in sour wine on a hyssop stalk to Jesus' lips.
nt.text: After this, knowing that everything had now been accomplished, and to fulfill the Scripture, Jesus said, “I am thirsty.” A jar of sour wine was sitting there. So they soaked a sponge in the wine, put it on a stalk of hyssop, and lifted it to His mouth. When Jesus had received the sour wine, He said, “It is finished.” And bowing His head, He yielded up His spirit. … they offered Him wine to drink, mixed with gall; but after tasting it, He refused to drink it.
nt.keyPhrase: to fulfill the Scripture, Jesus said, “I am thirsty.”

bridge: Notice the detail of the 'hyssop' stalk in John 19:29—the exact plant used in Exodus 12:22 to apply the Passover lamb's blood to the doorposts.

title: Not a Bone Broken & They Will Look on Him Whom They Pierced

ot.author: Moses, David & Zechariah
ot.context: The Passover lamb's bones may not be broken; a psalm of trust says 'not one of them will be broken'; through Zechariah God says, 'they will look on Me, the One they have pierced.'
ot.text: It must be eaten inside one house. You are not to take any of the meat outside the house, and you may not break any of the bones. … He protects all his bones; not one of them will be broken. … Then I will pour out on the house of David and on the people of Jerusalem a spirit of grace and prayer, and they will look on Me, the One they have pierced. They will mourn for Him as one mourns for an only child, and grieve bitterly for Him as one grieves for a firstborn son.
ot.keyPhrase: they will look on Me, the One they have pierced

nt.author: John
nt.context: The soldiers do not break Jesus' legs but pierce His side, and John cites two Scriptures as fulfilled; Revelation 1:7 applies Zechariah's words to Christ's return.
nt.text: But when they came to Jesus and saw that He was already dead, they did not break His legs. Instead, one of the soldiers pierced His side with a spear, and immediately blood and water flowed out. The one who saw it has testified to this, and his testimony is true. He knows that he is telling the truth, so that you also may believe. Now these things happened so that the Scripture would be fulfilled: “Not one of His bones will be broken.” And, as another Scripture says: “They will look on the One they have pierced.” … Behold, He is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see Him—even those who pierced Him. And all the tribes of the earth will mourn because of Him. So shall it be! Amen.
nt.keyPhrase: They will look on the One they have pierced

bridge: John sees two Scriptures fulfilled at the cross. The soldiers did not break Jesus' legs, and John cites 'Not one of His bones will be broken', which recalls the Passover rule that none of the lamb's bones may be broken and the psalm's 'not one of them will be broken'. Exodus gives a rule, not a prediction, so John reads it as typology (an earlier event or institution that foreshadows Christ), presenting Jesus as the true Passover lamb. For the spear thrust he cites Zechariah 12:10 in the form 'They will look on the One they have pierced.' In Zechariah God says 'they will look on Me' but then speaks of mourning 'for Him', and many Christians see here a hint of the Trinity (one God in three persons), though the New Testament does not draw this out.
keywords: Look on Him whom they pierced

title: Darkness at Noon on the Day of Crucifixion

ot.author: Amos
ot.context: Amos announces a day of judgment on Israel: the sun will go down at noon, and the land will mourn as for an only son.
ot.text: And in that day, declares the Lord GOD, I will make the sun go down at noon, and I will darken the earth in the daytime. I will turn your feasts into mourning and all your songs into lamentation. I will cause everyone to wear sackcloth and every head to be shaved. I will make it like a time of mourning for an only son, and its outcome like a bitter day.
ot.keyPhrase: I will make the sun go down at noon, and I will darken the earth in the daytime

nt.author: Matthew / Luke
nt.context: Darkness covers all the land from the sixth hour (noon) to the ninth hour (3 PM) while Jesus hangs on the cross.
nt.text: From the sixth hour until the ninth hour darkness came over all the land. … It was now about the sixth hour, and darkness came over all the land until the ninth hour. The sun was darkened, and the veil of the temple was torn down the middle.
nt.keyPhrase: From the sixth hour until the ninth hour darkness came over all the land

bridge: Amos announced a day of judgment when God would 'make the sun go down at noon' and turn Israel's feasts into mourning, 'like a time of mourning for an only son' (Amos 8:9-10). The Gospels report darkness over all the land from the sixth hour (noon) to the ninth (3 PM) while Jesus hung on the cross. They do not mention Amos, so the link is a parallel that readers draw: darkness at midday, and mourning as for an only son, at the death of the one a centurion called 'the Son of God' (Matthew 27:54). Some also recall the ninth plague, when darkness covered Egypt (Exodus 10:22). It cannot have been a solar eclipse: Passover fell at full moon, and the sun can only be eclipsed at new moon.

title: Buried in a Rich Man's Tomb

ot.author: Isaiah
ot.context: From Isaiah's poem of the suffering Servant: though He has done no violence, He is assigned a grave with the wicked and with a rich man in His death.
ot.text: He was assigned a grave with the wicked, and with a rich man in His death, although He had done no violence, nor was any deceit in His mouth.
ot.keyPhrase: with a rich man in His death

nt.author: Matthew
nt.context: Joseph of Arimathea, a rich disciple of Jesus, asks Pilate for the body and lays it in his own new tomb cut into the rock.
nt.text: When it was evening, there came a rich man from Arimathea named Joseph, who himself was a disciple of Jesus. He went to Pilate to ask for the body of Jesus, and Pilate ordered that it be given to him. So Joseph took the body, wrapped it in a clean linen cloth, and placed it in his own new tomb that he had cut into the rock. Then he rolled a great stone across the entrance to the tomb and went away.
nt.keyPhrase: there came a rich man from Arimathea named Joseph

bridge: Isaiah says the Servant 'was assigned a grave with the wicked, and with a rich man in His death'. Matthew, alone among the Gospel writers, calls Joseph of Arimathea 'a rich man', and Joseph lays the body of Jesus in 'his own new tomb that he had cut into the rock'. Many readers see a contrast here: a man executed between two robbers (Matthew 27:38), yet buried by a rich man. In Hebrew poetry, however, 'the wicked' and 'a rich man' may be two names for the same group, so the contrast is one possible reading, not a certain one. The New Testament does apply the second half of this verse, about the Servant's innocence, to Jesus (1 Peter 2:22).

title: The Holy One Will Not See Bodily Decay (The Resurrection)

ot.author: David
