ot.context: David's psalm of trust: with the LORD at his right hand, he is sure God will not abandon him to Sheol (the realm of the dead) or let His Holy One see decay.
ot.text: I have set the LORD always before me. Because He is at my right hand, I will not be shaken. Therefore my heart is glad and my tongue rejoices; my body also will dwell securely. For You will not abandon my soul to Sheol, nor will You let Your Holy One see decay. You have made known to me the path of life; You will fill me with joy in Your presence, with eternal pleasures at Your right hand.
ot.keyPhrase: nor will You let Your Holy One see decay

nt.author: Peter & Paul (Recorded by Luke)
nt.context: Peter's Pentecost sermon in Jerusalem and Paul's synagogue sermon in Pisidian Antioch.
nt.text: David says about Him: ‘I saw the Lord always before me; because He is at my right hand, I will not be shaken. Therefore my heart is glad and my tongue rejoices; my body also will dwell in hope, because You will not abandon my soul to Hades, nor will You let Your Holy One see decay. You have made known to me the paths of life; You will fill me with joy in Your presence.’ Brothers, I can tell you with confidence that the patriarch David died and was buried, and his tomb is with us to this day. But he was a prophet and knew that God had promised him on oath that He would place one of his descendants on his throne. Foreseeing this, David spoke about the resurrection of the Christ, that He was not abandoned to Hades, nor did His body see decay. God has raised this Jesus to life, to which we are all witnesses. … So also, He says in another Psalm: ‘You will not let Your Holy One see decay.’ For when David had served God’s purpose in his own generation, he fell asleep. His body was buried with his fathers and saw decay. But the One whom God raised from the dead did not see decay.
nt.keyPhrase: nor will You let Your Holy One see decay

bridge: In his Pentecost sermon Peter quotes Psalm 16:8-11 (Acts 2:25-28). He then reminds his hearers that David died and was buried, and his tomb was still there. So, Peter argues, David was speaking as a prophet about the resurrection of the Christ, whose body did not 'see decay'. Paul argues the same way in Pisidian Antioch: David 'saw decay', but 'the One whom God raised from the dead did not see decay' (Acts 13:36-37). Both apostles present the psalm as a prophecy fulfilled in the resurrection of Jesus.

title: The Sign of Jonah & Third-Day Resurrection

ot.author: Jonah & Hosea
ot.context: Jonah spends three days and three nights inside the great fish; in Hosea the people say God will revive them and raise them up 'on the third day'.
ot.text: Now the LORD had appointed a great fish to swallow Jonah, and Jonah spent three days and three nights in the belly of the fish. … After two days He will revive us; on the third day He will raise us up, that we may live in His presence.
ot.keyPhrase: three days and three nights in the belly of the fish

nt.author: Matthew / Paul
nt.context: Asked for a sign, Jesus offers only the sign of Jonah: the Son of Man will be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth. Paul says Christ was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures.
nt.text: Jesus replied, “A wicked and adulterous generation demands a sign, but none will be given it except the sign of the prophet Jonah. For as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so the Son of Man will be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth. … that He was buried, that He was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures,
nt.keyPhrase: as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish

bridge: Jesus Himself draws the comparison: 'as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so the Son of Man will be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth.' He adds that the people of Nineveh 'repented at the preaching of Jonah' (Matthew 12:41). This typology (a person or event that foreshadows Christ) is therefore Jesus' own: Jonah becomes a sign of His burial and rising. Paul says Christ was raised on the third day 'according to the Scriptures' (1 Corinthians 15:4) but does not name the passages he means. Hosea 6:2 is often suggested as one of them, though it speaks of Israel as a nation being revived 'on the third day', not of one person rising from the dead.

title: I Know That My Redeemer Lives & the Resurrection Hope

ot.author: Job
ot.context: At the lowest point of his suffering, Job declares that his Redeemer lives and that he will see God.
ot.text: But I know that my Redeemer lives, and in the end He will stand upon the earth. Even after my skin has been destroyed, yet in my flesh I will see God. I will see Him for myself; my eyes will behold Him, and not as a stranger. How my heart yearns within me!
ot.keyPhrase: I know that my Redeemer lives

nt.author: Paul
nt.context: Paul teaching that Christ has been raised and that the dead will be raised when the Lord returns.
nt.text: But Christ has indeed been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep. … in an instant, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, the dead will be raised imperishable, and we will be changed. For the perishable must be clothed with the imperishable, and the mortal with immortality. When the perishable has been clothed with the imperishable and the mortal with immortality, then the saying that is written will come to pass: “Death has been swallowed up in victory.” … For the Lord Himself will descend from heaven with a loud command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God, and the dead in Christ will be the first to rise.
nt.keyPhrase: Christ has indeed been raised from the dead

bridge: Job's story is usually set in the age of the patriarchs (Abraham, Isaac and Jacob), and many think it the oldest book in the Bible, but when it was written is unknown. In deep suffering Job says, 'I know that my Redeemer lives' (a redeemer, Hebrew go'el, was a relative who defended or rescued family), and he expects to see God. The New Testament never quotes or alludes to these words: Paul rests the resurrection hope on Christ's own resurrection, and the saying he quotes in 1 Corinthians 15:54 comes from Isaiah 25:8. The Hebrew of Job 19:26 is uncertain (it may mean seeing God 'in my flesh' or apart from it), so readers differ on whether Job expected bodily resurrection. Christians have long heard in his words a hope that Christ's resurrection answers, but this is a thematic parallel, not a fulfillment the New Testament claims.

title: The Stone the Builders Rejected Becomes the Cornerstone

ot.author: Psalmist & Isaiah
ot.context: A psalm of the Hallel (Psalms 113–118, sung at Passover) celebrating the rejected stone made the cornerstone; Isaiah 28:16 adds God's tested, precious cornerstone laid in Zion.
ot.text: The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone. This is from the LORD, and it is marvelous in our eyes. … So this is what the Lord GOD says: “See, I lay a stone in Zion, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, a sure foundation; the one who believes will never be shaken.
ot.keyPhrase: The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone

nt.author: Peter / Matthew
nt.context: Peter, on trial before the council that had condemned Jesus weeks earlier, names Him as the rejected stone; Jesus Himself quotes the psalm in Matthew 21:42, and 1 Peter joins it to Isaiah 28:16.
nt.text: then let this be known to all of you and to all the people of Israel: It is by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified but whom God raised from the dead, that this man stands before you healed. This Jesus is ‘the stone you builders rejected, which has become the cornerstone.’ … Jesus said to them, “Have you never read in the Scriptures: ‘The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone. This is from the Lord, and it is marvelous in our eyes’? … For it stands in Scripture: “See, I lay in Zion a stone, a chosen and precious cornerstone; and the one who believes in Him will never be put to shame.” To you who believe, then, this stone is precious. But to those who do not believe, “The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone,”
nt.keyPhrase: The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone

bridge: Psalm 118 celebrates a stone the builders threw aside that became the cornerstone (the key stone of a building). Jesus quotes it word for word in Matthew 21:42, and Peter tells the council that had condemned Jesus that He is 'the stone you builders rejected', the one God raised from the dead (Acts 4:10-11). 1 Peter 2:6-7 joins the psalm to Isaiah 28:16, God's promise of a precious cornerstone in Zion. Paul uses Isaiah's stone too (Romans 9:33), but not the psalm. In Peter's preaching the psalm explains how the leaders could reject the Messiah and how God reversed their verdict by raising Him.

title: Seated at God's Right Hand & Priest Forever Like Melchizedek

ot.author: David / Moses
ot.context: In David's psalm the LORD tells David's Lord to sit at His right hand and swears that He is a priest forever like Melchizedek, the king-priest who blessed Abraham (Genesis 14).
ot.text: A Psalm of David. The LORD said to my Lord: “Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet.” … The LORD has sworn and will not change His mind: “You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.” … Then Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine—since he was priest of God Most High— and he blessed Abram and said: “Blessed be Abram by God Most High, Creator of heaven and earth, and blessed be God Most High, who has delivered your enemies into your hand.” Then Abram gave Melchizedek a tenth of everything.
ot.keyPhrase: You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek

nt.author: Author of Hebrews / Peter (recorded by Luke)
nt.context: Peter's Pentecost sermon and the letter to the Hebrews apply Psalm 110 to the risen Jesus; Hebrews 7 retells Melchizedek's meeting with Abraham.
nt.text: This Melchizedek was king of Salem and priest of God Most High. He met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings and blessed him, and Abraham apportioned to him a tenth of everything. First, his name means “king of righteousness.” Then also, “king of Salem” means “king of peace.” Without father or mother or genealogy, without beginning of days or end of life, like the Son of God, he remains a priest for all time. … For it is testified: “You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.” … But because Jesus lives forever, He has a permanent priesthood. Therefore He is able to save completely those who draw near to God through Him, since He always lives to intercede for them. … Day after day every priest stands to minister and to offer again and again the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins. But when this Priest had offered for all time one sacrifice for sins, He sat down at the right hand of God. Since that time, He waits for His enemies to be made a footstool for His feet, … For David did not ascend into heaven, but he himself says: ‘The Lord said to my Lord, “Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet.”’ Therefore let all Israel know with certainty that God has made this Jesus, whom you crucified, both Lord and Christ!”
nt.keyPhrase: You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek

bridge: In Psalm 110 the LORD tells David's 'Lord' to sit at His right hand and swears that He is 'a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek'. Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, had once blessed Abraham (Genesis 14:18-20). In his Pentecost sermon, Peter quotes Psalm 110:1 to argue that David spoke not of himself but of Jesus, exalted to God's right hand (Acts 2:34-36). Hebrews 7 retells the Melchizedek story and quotes Psalm 110:4 to show that Jesus holds a permanent priesthood. Hebrews 10:11-13 then contrasts priests who stand day after day with Christ, who offered one sacrifice and 'sat down at the right hand of God'.

title: Ascended on High & Giving Gifts to Men

ot.author: David
ot.context: Triumphal procession of God ascending His holy mountain after routing His foes.
ot.text: You have ascended on high; You have led captives away. You have received gifts from men, even from the rebellious, that the LORD God may dwell there.
ot.keyPhrase: You have ascended on high; You have led captives away

nt.author: Paul
nt.context: Paul links the ascension of Christ with the gifts He gives to build up the church.
nt.text: This is why it says: “When He ascended on high, He led captives away, and gave gifts to men.” What does “He ascended” mean, except that He also descended to the lower parts of the earth? He who descended is the very One who ascended above all the heavens, in order to fill all things.
nt.keyPhrase: When He ascended on high, He led captives away, and gave gifts to men

bridge: Psalm 68 celebrates God going up to His holy mountain like a victorious king: 'You have ascended on high; You have led captives away. You have received gifts from men.' Paul quotes the verse and applies it to Christ, who 'ascended above all the heavens' (Ephesians 4:10). He changes one phrase: where the psalm says God received gifts from men, Paul writes that He 'gave gifts to men', a reading also found in some ancient Jewish interpretation of the psalm. The change suits his point: like a king sharing the spoils of victory, the risen Christ gives gifts to His people to build up the church (Ephesians 4:11-12).

title: The Son of Man Coming on the Clouds with Everlasting Dominion

ot.author: Daniel
ot.context: In a night vision Daniel sees One like the Son of Man come with the clouds of heaven to the Ancient of Days (God on His throne) and receive an everlasting kingdom that all nations will serve.
ot.text: In my vision in the night I continued to watch, and I saw One like the Son of Man coming with the clouds of heaven. He approached the Ancient of Days and was led into His presence. And He was given dominion, glory, and kingship, that the people of every nation and language should serve Him. His dominion is an everlasting dominion that will not pass away, and His kingdom is one that will never be destroyed.
ot.keyPhrase: One like the Son of Man coming with the clouds of heaven

nt.author: Matthew / John
nt.context: At His trial before the high priest Caiaphas, Jesus answers in Daniel's words; Revelation 1:7 announces that He is 'coming with the clouds', and John then sees 'One like the Son of Man'.
nt.text: “You have said it yourself,” Jesus answered. “But I say to all of you, from now on you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power and coming on the clouds of heaven.” … Behold, He is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see Him—even those who pierced Him. And all the tribes of the earth will mourn because of Him. So shall it be! Amen. … and among the lampstands was One like the Son of Man, dressed in a long robe, with a golden sash around His chest.
nt.keyPhrase: the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power and coming on the clouds of heaven

bridge: 'Son of Man' is the title Jesus most often uses for Himself. The phrase can simply mean a human being, as when God calls Ezekiel 'son of man' (Ezekiel 2:1), so not every saying points back to Daniel. At His trial, though, Jesus clearly draws on Daniel 7:13: they will see 'the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power and coming on the clouds of heaven'. In Daniel, One 'like the Son of Man' comes to the Ancient of Days and receives an everlasting kingdom. Yet Daniel 7:18, 27 give the kingdom to 'the saints of the Most High', so interpreters debate whether the figure is a heavenly king, a symbol of God's people, or both; the New Testament applies it to Jesus.

title: Death Swallowed Up in Victory

ot.author: Isaiah & Hosea
ot.context: Prophecy of the cosmic banquet on God's mountain where the shroud of death is destroyed forever.
ot.text: He will swallow up death forever. The Lord GOD will wipe away the tears from every face and remove the disgrace of His people from the whole earth. For the LORD has spoken. … I will ransom them from the power of Sheol; I will redeem them from Death. Where, O Death, are your plagues? Where, O Sheol, is your sting? Compassion is hidden from My eyes.
ot.keyPhrase: He will swallow up death forever

nt.author: Paul / John
nt.context: The climax of the resurrection chapter in 1 Corinthians 15 and the New Jerusalem in Revelation 21.
nt.text: When the perishable has been clothed with the imperishable and the mortal with immortality, then the saying that is written will come to pass: “Death has been swallowed up in victory.” “Where, O Death, is your victory? Where, O Death, is your sting?” … ‘He will wipe away every tear from their eyes,’ and there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain, for the former things have passed away.”
nt.keyPhrase: Death has been swallowed up in victory

bridge: Paul weaves Isaiah 25:8 and Hosea 13:14 into a single victory anthem over the grave, while John quotes the second half of Isaiah 25:8 ('wipe away every tear') in Revelation 21:4.

title: Every Knee Shall Bow and Every Tongue Confess

ot.author: Isaiah
ot.context: The most fiercely monotheistic speech in the Old Testament: Yahweh declares there is no other God besides Him.
ot.text: Turn to Me and be saved, all the ends of the earth; for I am God, and there is no other. By Myself I have sworn; truth has gone out from My mouth, a word that will not be revoked: Every knee will bow before Me, every tongue will swear allegiance.
ot.keyPhrase: Every knee will bow before Me, every tongue will swear allegiance

nt.author: Paul
nt.context: The Christ Hymn celebrating Jesus' exaltation after humbling Himself to the death of the Cross.
nt.text: Therefore God exalted Him to the highest place and gave Him the name above all names, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father. … It is written: “As surely as I live, says the Lord, every knee will bow before Me; every tongue will confess to God.”
nt.keyPhrase: at the name of Jesus every knee should bow

bridge: In Isaiah 45:23, Yahweh swears that every knee will bow exclusively to Him. In Philippians 2:10-11, Paul applies that exact monotheistic text to the risen Jesus, identifying 'Jesus Christ is Lord' with the divine name YHWH.

title: The Day of Atonement (Yom Kippur) & Entering Behind the Veil

ot.author: Moses
ot.context: Once a year, the High Priest enters the Holy of Holies with blood and lays Israel's sins on the scapegoat.
ot.text: Aaron shall then slaughter the goat for the sin offering for the people and bring its blood behind the veil, and with its blood he must do as he did with the bull’s blood: He is to sprinkle it against the mercy seat and in front of it. … Then he is to lay both hands on the head of the live goat and confess over it all the iniquities and rebellious acts of the Israelites in regard to all their sins. He is to put them on the goat’s head and send it away into the wilderness by the hand of a man appointed for the task. The goat will carry on itself all their iniquities into a solitary place, and the man will release it into the wilderness.
ot.keyPhrase: bring its blood behind the veil

nt.author: Author of Hebrews
nt.context: Hebrews presents Christ as the high priest who entered heaven itself once for all by His own blood and will appear a second time, opening a way for believers through the curtain.
nt.text: But when Christ came as high priest of the good things that have come, He went through the greater and more perfect tabernacle that is not made by hands and is not a part of this creation. He did not enter by the blood of goats and calves, but He entered the Most Holy Place once for all by His own blood, thus securing eternal redemption. … For Christ did not enter a man-made copy of the true sanctuary, but He entered heaven itself, now to appear on our behalf in the presence of God. … so also Christ was offered once to bear the sins of many; and He will appear a second time, not to bear sin, but to bring salvation to those who eagerly await Him. … Therefore, brothers, since we have confidence to enter the Most Holy Place by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way opened for us through the curtain of His body,
nt.keyPhrase: He entered the Most Holy Place once for all by His own blood

bridge: On the Day of Atonement the high priest brought the blood of the people's sin offering 'behind the veil' (Leviticus 16:15), then confessed Israel's sins over a live goat, which carried them away into the wilderness. Hebrews reads this day as a picture of Christ: He entered 'heaven itself', 'once for all by His own blood', and 'will appear a second time' (Hebrews 9:12, 24, 28). Believers may now enter by 'the new and living way' opened through the curtain (Hebrews 10:20). The New Testament never explicitly calls Christ the scapegoat (the goat sent away); Hebrews 13:11-12 compares His death outside the city gate with the sin-offering bodies burned outside the camp (Leviticus 16:27). Many also link the temple veil torn at His death (Matthew 27:51) with this day, though Matthew does not explain it.

title: The New Covenant Written on the Heart

ot.author: Jeremiah
ot.context: Promise of a New Covenant offering internal transformation and complete forgiveness of sins.
ot.text: Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah. It will not be like the covenant I made with their fathers when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt— a covenant they broke, though I was a husband to them,” declares the LORD. “But this is the covenant I will make with the house of Israel after those days, declares the LORD. I will put My law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts. And I will be their God, and they will be My people. No longer will each man teach his neighbor or his brother, saying, ‘Know the LORD,’ because they will all know Me, from the least of them to the greatest, declares the LORD. For I will forgive their iniquities and will remember their sins no more.”
ot.keyPhrase: I will put My law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts

nt.author: Luke / Hebrews / Paul
nt.context: Jesus instituting the New Covenant in His blood at the Last Supper; Paul describing Spirit-written hearts.
nt.text: In the same way, after supper He took the cup, saying, “This cup is the new covenant in My blood, which is poured out for you. … But God found fault with the people and said: “Behold, the days are coming, declares the Lord, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah. It will not be like the covenant I made with their fathers when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt, because they did not abide by My covenant, and I disregarded them, declares the Lord. For this is the covenant I will make with the house of Israel after those days, declares the Lord. I will put My laws in their minds and inscribe them on their hearts. And I will be their God, and they will be My people. No longer will each one teach his neighbor or his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord,’ because they will all know Me, from the least of them to the greatest. For I will forgive their iniquities and will remember their sins no more.” … It is clear that you are a letter from Christ, the result of our ministry, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts.
nt.keyPhrase: I will put My laws in their minds and inscribe them on their hearts

bridge: The Sinai Covenant gave an external standard on stone tablets but could not change the human heart; the New Covenant enacted by Jesus' blood writes God's desires within us by the Spirit.

title: A New Heart and My Spirit Within You

ot.author: Ezekiel
ot.context: God promising to cleanse His exiled people with clean water, replace their heart of stone, and place His Spirit within them.
ot.text: I will also sprinkle clean water on you, and you will be clean. I will cleanse you from all your impurities and all your idols. I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you; I will remove your heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh. And I will put My Spirit within you and cause you to walk in My statutes and to carefully observe My ordinances.
ot.keyPhrase: I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you

nt.author: John / Paul
nt.context: Jesus explaining to Nicodemus the new birth 'of water and the Spirit'; Paul writing of 'the washing of new birth' in Titus.
nt.text: Jesus answered, “Truly, truly, I tell you, no one can enter the kingdom of God unless he is born of water and the Spirit. Flesh is born of flesh, but spirit is born of the Spirit. Do not be amazed that I said, ‘You must be born again.’ The wind blows where it wishes. You hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it is going. So it is with everyone born of the Spirit.” … “You are Israel’s teacher,” said Jesus, “and you do not understand these things? … He saved us, not by the righteous deeds we had done, but according to His mercy, through the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit.
nt.keyPhrase: unless he is born of water and the Spirit

bridge: Jesus tells Nicodemus that no one can enter God's kingdom 'unless he is born of water and the Spirit', and asks how Israel's teacher can 'not understand these things' (John 3:10). He does not cite a verse, but many readers think He has Ezekiel 36:25-27 in mind. There God promises to sprinkle clean water on His people, give them a new heart and put His Spirit within them. Titus 3:5 speaks in a similar way of 'the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit' (new birth is also called regeneration). On this reading, being born again is the inner renewal the prophets promised.

title: The Outpouring of the Holy Spirit on All Flesh

ot.author: Joel
ot.context: Prophecy that God will pour out His Spirit beyond kings and prophets onto sons, daughters, and servants.
ot.text: And afterward, I will pour out My Spirit on all people. Your sons and daughters will prophesy, your old men will dream dreams, your young men will see visions. Even on My menservants and maidservants, I will pour out My Spirit in those days. I will show wonders in the heavens and on the earth, blood and fire and columns of smoke. The sun will be turned to darkness and the moon to blood before the coming of the great and awesome Day of the LORD. And everyone who calls on the name of the LORD will be saved; for on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there will be deliverance, as the LORD has promised, among the remnant called by the LORD.
ot.keyPhrase: I will pour out My Spirit on all people

nt.author: Peter (Recorded by Luke) / Paul
nt.context: Day of Pentecost in Jerusalem as the Holy Spirit descends upon the disciples.
nt.text: No, this is what was spoken by the prophet Joel: ‘In the last days, God says, I will pour out My Spirit on all people. Your sons and daughters will prophesy, your young men will see visions, your old men will dream dreams. Even on My menservants and maidservants I will pour out My Spirit in those days, and they will prophesy. I will show wonders in the heavens above and signs on the earth below, blood and fire and billows of smoke. The sun will be turned to darkness, and the moon to blood, before the coming of the great and glorious Day of the Lord. And everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.’ … for, “Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.”
nt.keyPhrase: I will pour out My Spirit on all people

bridge: In the Old Testament, the Spirit came upon select leaders for specific tasks. Joel foretold the democratized outpouring of the Spirit upon all believers—fulfilled on Pentecost and linked to calling on the name of Jesus (Rom 10:9-13).

title: The Just Shall Live by His Faith

ot.author: Habakkuk
ot.context: God's answer to Habakkuk on the watchtower as Babylonian judgment approaches.
ot.text: Look at the proud one; his soul is not upright— but the righteous will live by faith—
ot.keyPhrase: the righteous will live by faith

nt.author: Paul / Author of Hebrews
nt.context: Paul quotes the line in the theme statement of Romans and in his case against justification by the law in Galatians; Hebrews uses it to urge endurance.
nt.text: For the gospel reveals the righteousness of God that comes by faith from start to finish, just as it is written: “The righteous will live by faith.” … Now it is clear that no one is justified before God by the law, because, “The righteous will live by faith.” … But My righteous one will live by faith; and if he shrinks back, I will take no pleasure in him.”
nt.keyPhrase: The righteous will live by faith

bridge: God answers Habakkuk's complaint about the coming Babylonian invasion with a short line, only three words in Hebrew: 'the righteous will live by faith'. In context it promises that the righteous will come through the judgment by trusting God and staying faithful; the Hebrew word can mean both faith and faithfulness. Paul quotes it in Romans 1:17 and Galatians 3:11 to show that people are justified (declared right with God) by faith, not by keeping the law. Hebrews 10:38 quotes it to urge believers to endure and not shrink back. Preachers sometimes match each book to one part of the line, but that is a teaching outline, not something the texts themselves state.

title: Rebuilding David's Fallen Tent to Include All Nations

ot.author: Amos
ot.context: Amos closes with God's promise to restore the fallen tent of David, so that Israel will possess the remnant of Edom and all the nations that bear God's name.
ot.text: “In that day I will restore the fallen tent of David. I will repair its gaps, restore its ruins, and rebuild it as in the days of old, that they may possess the remnant of Edom and all the nations that bear My name,” declares the LORD, who will do this.
ot.keyPhrase: I will restore the fallen tent of David

nt.author: James (at the Jerusalem Council, recorded by Luke)
nt.context: James quotes Amos at the Jerusalem Council, which decides that Gentile believers need not be circumcised to belong to God's people.
nt.text: The words of the prophets agree with this, as it is written: ‘After this I will return and rebuild the fallen tent of David. Its ruins I will rebuild, and I will restore it, so that the remnant of men may seek the Lord, and all the Gentiles who are called by My name, says the Lord who does these things that have been known for ages.’
nt.keyPhrase: I will return and rebuild the fallen tent of David

bridge: Amos ends with a promise that God will rebuild 'the fallen tent of David', usually taken to mean David's royal house, which had fallen into ruin. At the Jerusalem Council, a meeting of apostles and elders about whether Gentile believers must be circumcised (Acts 15:5), James quotes this promise. He follows the Septuagint (the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament), so Acts 15:17 reads 'so that the remnant of men may seek the Lord'; the Hebrew-based text of Amos says 'that they may possess the remnant of Edom'. Both versions speak of nations called by God's name. James concludes that God is taking a people for Himself from the Gentiles, so they should not be burdened (Acts 15:14, 19).

title: The Latter Glory of This House & the Unshakable Kingdom

ot.author: Haggai
ot.context: Haggai encourages the builders of the Second Temple, which looked like nothing beside Solomon's, with God's promise of greater glory.
ot.text: For this is what the LORD of Hosts says: “Once more, in a little while, I will shake the heavens and the earth, the sea and the dry land. I will shake all the nations, and they will come with all their treasures, and I will fill this house with glory, says the LORD of Hosts. The silver is Mine, and the gold is Mine, declares the LORD of Hosts. The latter glory of this house will be greater than the former, says the LORD of Hosts. And in this place I will provide peace, declares the LORD of Hosts.”
ot.keyPhrase: Once more, in a little while, I will shake the heavens and the earth

nt.author: Author of Hebrews / Luke / John
nt.context: Hebrews applies Haggai's shaking to God's unshakable kingdom; Simeon holds the infant Jesus in the temple courts; Jesus speaks of His body as a temple.
nt.text: At that time His voice shook the earth, but now He has promised, “Once more I will shake not only the earth, but heaven as well.” The words “Once more” signify the removal of what can be shaken—that is, created things—so that the unshakable may remain. Therefore, since we are receiving an unshakable kingdom, let us be filled with gratitude, and so worship God acceptably with reverence and awe. … Led by the Spirit, he went into the temple courts. And when the parents brought in the child Jesus to do for Him what was customary under the Law, Simeon took Him in his arms and blessed God, saying: “Sovereign Lord, as You have promised, You now dismiss Your servant in peace. For my eyes have seen Your salvation, which You have prepared in the sight of all people, a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to Your people Israel.” … Jesus answered, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up again.” “This temple took forty-six years to build,” the Jews replied, “and You are going to raise it up in three days?” But Jesus was speaking about the temple of His body.
nt.keyPhrase: Once more I will shake not only the earth, but heaven as well

bridge: Haggai encourages the builders of the Second Temple (rebuilt after the exile), which looked like nothing beside Solomon's (Haggai 2:3), with God's promise: He will 'shake the heavens and the earth', the nations 'will come with all their treasures', and 'the latter glory of this house will be greater than the former'. Hebrews 12:26-28 quotes the first of these lines and applies it to the removal of created things, so that only God's unshakable kingdom remains. Christians have long seen the greater glory in the presence of Jesus in that temple, where Simeon took Him in his arms as an infant (Luke 2:27-28), and in Jesus calling His body a temple (John 2:21), but neither passage mentions Haggai. Older translations rendered part of Haggai 2:7 as the coming of the Desire of All Nations, often read as a title of the Messiah; the Hebrew speaks of the treasures of the nations.

title: Divine Wisdom Present at Creation

ot.author: Solomon
ot.context: Wisdom, pictured as a woman, says she was with the LORD before the world began and at His side as He made the heavens, the sea and the earth.
ot.text: The LORD created me as His first course, before His works of old. From everlasting I was established, from the beginning, before the earth began. When there were no watery depths, I was brought forth, when no springs were overflowing with water. Before the mountains were settled, before the hills, I was brought forth, before He made the land or fields, or any of the dust of the earth. I was there when He established the heavens, when He inscribed a circle on the face of the deep, when He established the clouds above, when the fountains of the deep gushed forth, when He set a boundary for the sea, so that the waters would not surpass His command, when He marked out the foundations of the earth. Then I was a skilled craftsman at His side, and His delight day by day, rejoicing always in His presence. I was rejoicing in His whole world, delighting together in the sons of men.
ot.keyPhrase: I was there when He established the heavens

nt.author: Paul / John
nt.context: Paul and John describe Christ as the one through whom all things were made; Paul also calls Christ 'the wisdom of God'.
nt.text: The Son is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn over all creation. For in Him all things were created, things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities. All things were created through Him and for Him. He is before all things, and in Him all things hold together. … but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God. … In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was with God in the beginning. Through Him all things were made, and without Him nothing was made that has been made.
nt.keyPhrase: All things were created through Him and for Him

bridge: In Proverbs 8 Wisdom speaks as a person, a figure of speech called personification. She says she was with the LORD before the world began, 'a skilled craftsman at His side' as He made the heavens and the sea. No New Testament passage quotes Proverbs 8, but John 1:1-3, speaking of the Word (Greek Logos), and Colossians 1:15-17 describe Christ in similar terms: with God in the beginning, before all things, the one through whom all things were made. Many scholars think these writers drew on the Jewish picture of Wisdom, and Paul calls Christ 'the wisdom of God', though there he means the message of the cross (1 Corinthians 1:18-24). Yet the New Testament never quotes Proverbs 8:22, where the LORD 'created' Wisdom (the Hebrew verb can also mean 'acquired'); it borrows Wisdom's role in creation, not that verse.

title: Solomon's Temple Prayer for the Foreigner & House of Prayer

ot.author: Solomon & Isaiah
ot.context: At the dedication of the first temple, Solomon prays that foreigners from distant lands will come to know God's name; Isaiah promises that God's house will be called a house of prayer for all the nations.
ot.text: And as for the foreigner who is not of Your people Israel but has come from a distant land because of Your name— for they will hear of Your great name and mighty hand and outstretched arm—when he comes and prays toward this temple, then may You hear from heaven, Your dwelling place, and do according to all for which the foreigner calls to You. Then all the peoples of the earth will know Your name and fear You, as do Your people Israel, and they will know that this house I have built is called by Your Name. … I will bring them to My holy mountain and make them joyful in My house of prayer. Their burnt offerings and sacrifices will be accepted on My altar, for My house will be called a house of prayer for all the nations.”
ot.keyPhrase: My house will be called a house of prayer for all the nations

nt.author: Mark / Paul
nt.context: Clearing the temple courts, Jesus quotes Isaiah 56:7; Paul tells Gentiles who were once far away that they are now fellow citizens, built into God's holy temple.
nt.text: Then Jesus began to teach them, and He declared, “Is it not written: ‘My house will be called a house of prayer for all the nations’? But you have made it ‘a den of robbers.’” … But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far away have been brought near through the blood of Christ. … Therefore you are no longer strangers and foreigners, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household, built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus Himself as the cornerstone. In Him the whole building is fitted together and grows into a holy temple in the Lord. And in Him you too are being built together into a dwelling place for God in His Spirit.
nt.keyPhrase: My house will be called a house of prayer for all the nations

bridge: At the temple's dedication Solomon asks God to hear the foreigner who comes 'from a distant land because of Your name', so that 'all the peoples of the earth will know Your name'. Isaiah later promises such foreigners a welcome, 'for My house will be called a house of prayer for all the nations' (Isaiah 56:6-7). Clearing the temple courts, Jesus asks 'Is it not written' and quotes Isaiah's words, adding Jeremiah's 'den of robbers' (Jeremiah 7:11). The trading was probably in the outer court of Herod's temple, the only part Gentiles could enter, so many read His protest as defending the nations' place of prayer. Ephesians 2 does not quote these texts but shares their hope: Gentiles who were once 'far away have been brought near' and are built into 'a holy temple in the Lord'.

title: The Bridegroom and the Bride (The Royal Wedding Song)

ot.author: Moses, the Sons of Korah & Solomon
ot.context: Marriage as one flesh (Genesis 2:24), a love song for a royal wedding (Psalm 45) and the love poetry of the Song of Songs.
ot.text: For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and they will become one flesh. … Your throne, O God, endures forever and ever, and justice is the scepter of Your kingdom. You have loved righteousness and hated wickedness; therefore God, your God, has anointed you above your companions with the oil of joy. … My beloved is mine and I am his; he pastures his flock among the lilies.
ot.keyPhrase: a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife

nt.author: Paul / Author of Hebrews / John
nt.context: Paul applying Genesis 2:24 to Christ and the church, Hebrews applying Psalm 45:6-7 to the Son, and Revelation's marriage of the Lamb.
nt.text: Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her … “For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and the two will become one flesh.” This mystery is profound, but I am speaking about Christ and the church. … But about the Son He says: “Your throne, O God, endures forever and ever, and justice is the scepter of Your kingdom. You have loved righteousness and hated wickedness; therefore God, Your God, has anointed You above Your companions with the oil of joy.” … Let us rejoice and be glad and give Him the glory. For the marriage of the Lamb has come, and His bride has made herself ready. She was given clothing of fine linen, bright and pure.” For the fine linen she wears is the righteous acts of the saints. Then the angel told me to write, “Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb.” And he said to me, “These are the true words of God.”
nt.keyPhrase: a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife

bridge: In Ephesians 5:31-32 Paul quotes Genesis 2:24 on marriage and then says, 'This mystery is profound, but I am speaking about Christ and the church' (for Paul, a mystery is a truth once hidden and now revealed). The New Testament thus reads marriage as typology (an earlier institution that foreshadows Christ): a picture of Christ and the church. Revelation 19 uses the same picture: 'the marriage of the Lamb has come, and His bride has made herself ready'. Psalm 45 is a song for a royal wedding, and Hebrews 1:8-9 applies its verses 6-7 to the Son, but to His throne, not to a bride. No New Testament text quotes the Song of Songs; reading it as a picture of Christ and His people is a long Christian tradition of allegory (reading a text as a picture of a deeper truth), not a link the New Testament makes.

title: Creation Subjected to Vanity & Longing for Redemption

ot.author: Solomon (Qoheleth)
ot.context: The Teacher (Qoheleth) calls everything hevel, futility or literally 'breath', and asks what people gain from all their toil 'under the sun'.
ot.text: “Futility of futilities,” says the Teacher, “futility of futilities! Everything is futile!” What does a man gain from all his labor, at which he toils under the sun?
ot.keyPhrase: Futility of futilities

nt.author: Paul
nt.context: Paul says creation 'was subjected to futility' in hope of being set free, using the Greek Old Testament's word for Ecclesiastes' refrain; elsewhere he tells believers their labor in the Lord is not in vain.
nt.text: For the creation was subjected to futility, not by its own will, but because of the One who subjected it, in hope that the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to decay and brought into the glorious freedom of the children of God. … Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast and immovable. Always excel in the work of the Lord, because you know that your labor in the Lord is not in vain.
nt.keyPhrase: the creation was subjected to futility

bridge: Ecclesiastes sums up life 'under the sun' with one Hebrew word, hevel (futility, literally 'breath'): 'Everything is futile!' The Septuagint (the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament) renders it mataiotēs, the same word Paul uses when he says 'the creation was subjected to futility' in hope of being set free. Whether Paul had Ecclesiastes in mind is uncertain; the clearer background to Romans 8:20 is the curse on the ground after the Fall (Genesis 3:17-19). Read side by side, the two books make a striking pair: the Teacher asks what people gain from all their labor, and Paul assures believers that their 'labor in the Lord is not in vain', though there he uses a different Greek word that simply means empty.

title: Deliverers Raised Up by the LORD & Strength from Weakness

ot.author: Anonymous (Jewish tradition: Samuel)
ot.context: The LORD raises up judges to rescue Israel: the angel greets Gideon as a 'mighty man of valor', and Samson dies bringing the Philistines' temple down on them.
ot.text: Then the LORD raised up judges, who saved them from the hands of those who plundered them. … And the angel of the LORD appeared to Gideon and said, “The LORD is with you, O mighty man of valor.” … Samson said, “Let me die with the Philistines.” Then he pushed with all his might, and the temple fell on the lords and all the people in it. So in his death he killed more than he had killed in his life.
ot.keyPhrase: in his death he killed more than he had killed in his life

nt.author: Author of Hebrews
nt.context: Hebrews 11 (often called the Hall of Faith) names Gideon, Barak and Samson among those who acted by faith; Hebrews 2:14 says Jesus shared our humanity so that by His death He might destroy the devil.
nt.text: And what more shall I say? Time will not allow me to tell of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel, and the prophets, who through faith conquered kingdoms, administered justice, and gained what was promised; who shut the mouths of lions, quenched the raging fire, and escaped the edge of the sword; who gained strength from weakness, became mighty in battle, and put foreign armies to flight. … Now since the children have flesh and blood, He too shared in their humanity, so that by His death He might destroy him who holds the power of death, that is, the devil,
nt.keyPhrase: who gained strength from weakness

bridge: In Judges, 'the LORD raised up judges' to rescue Israel from its enemies (Judges 2:16). Hebrews 11:32-34 names Gideon, Barak and Samson among those who acted through faith and 'gained strength from weakness'. Hebrews holds them up as examples of faith; it does not call them pictures of Christ. Their victories often came against the odds: Gideon's army was cut to three hundred men (Judges 7:7), and Samson killed more at his death than in his life (Judges 16:30). Christians have long seen in such rescues, and above all in Samson's death, a faint picture of Christ, who by dying would 'destroy him who holds the power of death' (Hebrews 2:14); that link comes from later Christian reading, not from the New Testament.

title: Return from Exile: Rebuilding God's House & Understanding the Scriptures

ot.author: Ezra & Nehemiah
ot.context: Cyrus allows the exiles to return and rebuild the LORD's house in Jerusalem; later Ezra and the Levites read the Law aloud and explain it so the people understand.
ot.text: In the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, to fulfill the word of the LORD spoken through Jeremiah, the LORD stirred the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia to send a proclamation throughout his kingdom and to put it in writing as follows: “This is what Cyrus king of Persia says: ‘The LORD, the God of heaven, who has given me all the kingdoms of the earth, has appointed me to build a house for Him at Jerusalem in Judah. Whoever among you belongs to His people, may his God be with him, and may he go to Jerusalem in Judah and build the house of the LORD, the God of Israel; He is the God who is in Jerusalem. … So they read from the Book of the Law of God, explaining it and giving insight, so that the people could understand what was being read.
ot.keyPhrase: so that the people could understand what was being read

nt.author: Luke / Peter
nt.context: The risen Jesus opens the minds of the disciples to understand the Scriptures, and Peter describes believers as living stones built into a spiritual house.
nt.text: Jesus said to them, “These are the words I spoke to you while I was still with you: Everything must be fulfilled that is written about Me in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms.” Then He opened their minds to understand the Scriptures. … you also, like living stones, are being built into a spiritual house to be a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.
nt.keyPhrase: He opened their minds to understand the Scriptures

bridge: After the exile, Cyrus king of Persia lets the Jews return to 'build the house of the LORD' in Jerusalem, and later Ezra and the Levites read the Law aloud, explaining it 'so that the people could understand what was being read'. The New Testament never quotes or names Ezra or Nehemiah, so this pairing is a thematic parallel (a link drawn by the app, not by the New Testament). Two of its themes do return there: the risen Jesus, speaking of what is written about Him in the Law of Moses, the Prophets and the Psalms, 'opened their minds to understand the Scriptures' (Luke 24:44-45), and Peter tells believers that 'like living stones' they 'are being built into a spiritual house' (1 Peter 2:5). Christians may see God rebuilding His people in both stories, but that is a reading for reflection and prayer, not a connection the texts themselves make.

title: For Such a Time as This: Royal Intercession Saving the Covenant People

ot.author: Mordecai & Esther (author of the book unknown)
ot.context: Queen Esther risking her life to enter the king's inner court unbidden to save her people from Haman's decree of annihilation.
ot.text: For if you remain silent at this time, relief and deliverance for the Jews will arise from another place, but you and your father’s house will perish. And who knows if perhaps you have come to the kingdom for such a time as this?” Then Esther sent this reply to Mordecai: “Go and assemble all the Jews who can be found in Susa, and fast for me. Do not eat or drink for three days, night or day, and I and my maidens will fast as you do. After that, I will go to the king, even though it is against the law. And if I perish, I perish!” … For how could I bear to see the disaster that would befall my people? How could I bear to see the destruction of my kindred?”
ot.keyPhrase: I will go to the king, even though it is against the law. And if I perish, I perish!

nt.author: Author of Hebrews / Paul
nt.context: Hebrews invites believers to approach God's throne of grace with confidence; Paul says the risen Christ is at God's right hand and intercedes for us.
nt.text: Let us then approach the throne of grace with confidence, so that we may receive mercy and find grace to help us in our time of need. … Who is there to condemn us? For Christ Jesus, who died, and more than that was raised to life, is at the right hand of God—and He is interceding for us.
nt.keyPhrase: Let us then approach the throne of grace with confidence

bridge: When Haman's decree condemned every Jew in the Persian empire (Esther 3:13), Mordecai told Queen Esther she might have come to the kingdom 'for such a time as this'. She resolved to go to the king unsummoned, against the law: 'And if I perish, I perish!' The book never names God, but many readers see His hidden care in the rescue of the people from whom the Messiah would later come. The New Testament never quotes or mentions Esther, so linking her to Christ is a parallel the app draws, best read as a contrast. Esther approached an earthly throne at the risk of her life, while Hebrews 4:16 invites believers to 'approach the throne of grace with confidence', and Paul says the risen Christ 'is interceding for us' (Romans 8:34).

title: Lamentations Over Fallen Jerusalem & Mercies New Every Morning

ot.author: Jeremiah (trad.)
ot.context: The poet of Lamentations (traditionally Jeremiah) mourns Jerusalem's destruction, yet anchors hope in the LORD's mercies that never fail.
ot.text: All who pass by clap their hands at you in scorn. They hiss and shake their heads at the Daughter of Jerusalem: “Is this the city that was called the perfection of beauty, the joy of all the earth?” … Because of the loving devotion of the LORD we are not consumed, for His mercies never fail. They are new every morning; great is Your faithfulness!
ot.keyPhrase: All who pass by clap their hands at you in scorn. They hiss and shake their heads

nt.author: Luke / Matthew / Paul
nt.context: Jesus weeping over Jerusalem on Palm Sunday; passersby shaking their heads at the Cross; Christ remaining faithful.
nt.text: As Jesus approached Jerusalem and saw the city, He wept over it and said, “If only you had known on this day what would bring you peace! But now it is hidden from your eyes. For the days will come upon you when your enemies will barricade you and surround you and hem you in on every side. They will level you to the ground—you and the children within your walls. They will not leave one stone on another, because you did not recognize the time of your visitation from God.” … And those who passed by heaped abuse on Him, shaking their heads … if we are faithless, He remains faithful, for He cannot deny Himself.
nt.keyPhrase: those who passed by heaped abuse on Him, shaking their heads

bridge: Lamentations mourns Jerusalem after its fall in 586 BC: passers-by 'hiss and shake their heads at the Daughter of Jerusalem', yet the poet still says to the LORD, 'great is Your faithfulness!' Centuries later Jesus weeps over the same city as He foretells its destruction (Luke 19:41-44). At the cross 'those who passed by' shake their heads at Him (Matthew 27:39); the scene draws mainly on Psalm 22:7, but the passers-by may also echo Lamentations 2:15. Paul's 'He remains faithful' (2 Timothy 2:13) shares the hope of Lamentations 3:22-23. These are parallels in theme; the New Testament does not quote Lamentations here.

title: The Kingdom Shall Be the Lord's & the Herald of Good News

ot.author: Obadiah & Nahum
ot.context: Oracles against Edom and Nineveh: the Day of the LORD near for all nations, a messenger bringing Judah news of peace, and the kingdom belonging to the LORD.
ot.text: For the Day of the LORD is near for all the nations. As you have done, it will be done to you; your recompense will return upon your own head. … The deliverers will ascend Mount Zion to rule over the mountains of Esau. And the kingdom will belong to the LORD. … Look to the mountains— the feet of one who brings good news, who proclaims peace! Celebrate your feasts, O Judah; fulfill your vows. For the wicked will never again march through you; they will be utterly cut off.
ot.keyPhrase: the kingdom will belong to the LORD

nt.author: John / Paul
nt.context: The seventh trumpet announcing that the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ; Paul on the feet of those who bring good news.
nt.text: Then the seventh angel sounded his trumpet, and loud voices called out in heaven: “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ, and He will reign forever and ever.” … And how can they preach unless they are sent? As it is written: “How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news!”
nt.keyPhrase: The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ

bridge: No New Testament text cites Obadiah or Nahum, so this is a thematic parallel drawn by the app. Nahum 1:15 pictures a messenger on the mountains bringing Judah news of peace, because its Assyrian enemy will be cut off. Romans 10:15 uses almost the same words for preachers of the gospel, but Paul is quoting Isaiah 52:7, a near twin of Nahum's verse: 'How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of those who bring good news'. Obadiah warns that the Day of the LORD is near for all nations and ends with 'the kingdom will belong to the LORD'. Revelation 11:15 announces 'the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ'; it may echo Obadiah, but it shares this hope with other passages such as Psalm 2:2 and Daniel 7:14.

title: The Lord Singing Over His People in Zion

ot.author: Zephaniah
ot.context: After the purifying judgment of the Day of the Lord, God Himself rejoices over His people with singing.
ot.text: Sing for joy, O Daughter of Zion; shout aloud, O Israel! Be glad and rejoice with all your heart, O Daughter of Jerusalem! The LORD has taken away your punishment; He has turned back your enemy. Israel’s King, the LORD, is among you; no longer will you fear any harm. On that day they will say to Jerusalem: “Do not fear, O Zion; do not let your hands fall limp. The LORD your God is among you; He is mighty to save. He will rejoice over you with gladness; He will quiet you with His love; He will rejoice over you with singing.”
ot.keyPhrase: Do not fear, O Zion

nt.author: John
nt.context: Jesus rides into Jerusalem as Zion's King and John cites Scripture, 'Do not be afraid, O Daughter of Zion'; in John's final vision God comes to live among His people.
nt.text: “Do not be afraid, O Daughter of Zion. See, your King is coming, seated on the colt of a donkey.” … And I heard a loud voice from the throne saying: “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them. They will be His people, and God Himself will be with them as their God.
nt.keyPhrase: Do not be afraid, O Daughter of Zion. See, your King is coming

bridge: Zephaniah ends with a call to the Daughter of Zion to sing for joy, because the LORD, Israel's King, is among her, and with a striking picture: God Himself 'will rejoice over you with singing'. When Jesus rides into Jerusalem, John cites Scripture: 'Do not be afraid, O Daughter of Zion. See, your King is coming'. Most of this comes from Zechariah 9:9, but the opening words may borrow from Zephaniah 3:16 ('Do not fear, O Zion'), though Isaiah 40:9 is another possible source. Revelation 21:3 shares Zephaniah's hope of God living among His people. But no New Testament text speaks of God singing over His people, so that part of the link is thematic, not one the New Testament makes.

title: Elijah Sent Ahead & the Rising Sun of Righteousness

ot.author: Malachi
ot.context: The closing words of Malachi, the last book of the Christian Old Testament: the sun of righteousness will rise, and Elijah will come before the day of the LORD.
ot.text: “But for you who fear My name, the sun of righteousness will rise with healing in its wings, and you will go out and leap like calves from the stall. … Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and awesome Day of the LORD. And he will turn the hearts of the fathers to their children, and the hearts of the children to their fathers. Otherwise, I will come and strike the land with a curse.”
ot.keyPhrase: he will turn the hearts of the fathers to their children

nt.author: Luke / Matthew / Peter
nt.context: The angel's words about John the Baptist, Zechariah's song of the Dawn from on high, a woman touching the fringe of Jesus' cloak, and Peter's morning star.
nt.text: And he will go on before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of the fathers to their children and the disobedient to the wisdom of the righteous—to make ready a people prepared for the Lord.” … because of the tender mercy of our God, by which the Dawn will visit us from on high, to shine on those who live in darkness and in the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the path of peace.” … Suddenly a woman who had suffered from bleeding for twelve years came up behind Him and touched the fringe of His cloak. … We also have the word of the prophets as confirmed beyond doubt. And you will do well to pay attention to it, as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts.
nt.keyPhrase: in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of the fathers to their children

bridge: Malachi closes with two promises: 'the sun of righteousness will rise with healing in its wings', and God will send 'Elijah the prophet' before the day of the LORD. Luke 1:17 applies the second to John the Baptist, who will go 'in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of the fathers to their children'. The Dawn from on high in Luke 1:78 and the morning star of 2 Peter 1:19 may echo Malachi's sunrise, though other texts, such as the star of Numbers 24:17, are also proposed. Malachi's 'wings' are usually read as the sun's rays, but some modern teachers link them to the fringe of the cloak a sick woman touched (Matthew 9:20), since the Hebrew word for wings also means a garment's corners, where tassels hung (Numbers 15:38). Matthew never mentions Malachi, and his Greek word for the fringe is not the word for 'wings' in the Greek translation of Malachi.

title: The Worker's Wages & the Lord Who Knows His Own

ot.author: Moses
ot.context: A law that an ox treading out grain must not be muzzled, and the words of Moses to Korah and his rebels: the LORD will reveal who belongs to Him.
ot.text: Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain. … Then he said to Korah and all his followers, “Tomorrow morning the LORD will reveal who belongs to Him and who is holy, and He will bring that person near to Himself. The one He chooses, He will bring near to Himself.
ot.keyPhrase: Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain

nt.author: Paul
nt.context: Paul asks that elders who preach and teach be supported, and assures Timothy that God's firm foundation stands despite false teachers.
nt.text: Elders who lead effectively are worthy of double honor, especially those who work hard at preaching and teaching. For the Scripture says, “Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain,” and, “The worker is worthy of his wages.” … Nevertheless, God’s firm foundation stands, bearing this seal: “The Lord knows those who are His,” and, “Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord must turn away from iniquity.”
nt.keyPhrase: Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain

bridge: Paul introduces the law of Moses 'Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain' with 'For the Scripture says' and uses it to argue for supporting elders who work hard at preaching and teaching (1 Timothy 5:17). He adds 'The worker is worthy of his wages', words Jesus speaks in Luke 10:7; whether 'the Scripture says' is meant to cover this second saying too is debated. In 2 Timothy 2:19, after warning about false teachers (2 Timothy 2:17-18), Paul says that God's firm foundation bears the seal 'The Lord knows those who are His', which follows the words of Moses to Korah in Numbers 16:5, most closely in the Septuagint (the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament).

title: Old Testament Echoes in the Letters of John, Peter and Jude

ot.author: Moses & Zechariah
ot.context: The command to love your neighbor as yourself (Leviticus 19:18), the LORD rebuking Satan in Zechariah's vision (Zechariah 3:2), and a prayer of Moses that a thousand years are like a day to God (Psalm 90:4).
ot.text: Do not seek revenge or bear a grudge against any of your people, but love your neighbor as yourself. I am the LORD. … And the LORD said to Satan: “The LORD rebukes you, Satan! Indeed, the LORD, who has chosen Jerusalem, rebukes you! Is not this man a firebrand snatched from the fire?” … For in Your sight a thousand years are but a day that passes, or a watch of the night.
ot.keyPhrase: The LORD rebukes you, Satan!

nt.author: John, Peter & Jude
nt.context: John urges believers to love one another; Peter reminds them that with the Lord a day is like a thousand years; Jude tells how the archangel Michael left the rebuke of the devil to the Lord.
nt.text: And love consists in this: not that we loved God, but that He loved us and sent His Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins. Beloved, if God so loved us, we also ought to love one another. … And now I urge you, dear lady—not as a new commandment to you, but one we have had from the beginning—that we love one another. And this is love, that we walk according to His commandments. This is the very commandment you have heard from the beginning, that you must walk in love. … Beloved, do not let this one thing escape your notice: With the Lord a day is like a thousand years, and a thousand years are like a day. … But even the archangel Michael, when he disputed with the devil over the body of Moses, did not presume to bring a slanderous charge against him, but said, “The Lord rebuke you!”
nt.keyPhrase: The Lord rebuke you!

bridge: The General Letters (the New Testament letters from James to Jude) often echo the Old Testament without formally quoting it. In Jude 1:9 the archangel Michael, in a Jewish tradition about the body of Moses, says 'The Lord rebuke you!', the words the LORD speaks to Satan in Zechariah 3:2. Peter's reminder that 'a day is like a thousand years' (2 Peter 3:8) echoes Psalm 90:4. The call to 'love one another' in 1 and 2 John repeats Jesus' command in John 13:34. It shares the idea of Leviticus 19:18, 'love your neighbor as yourself', but John does not quote that verse.

title: From Eden's Tree of Life to the New Heaven, New Earth & River of Life
eraGap: c. 1400 / 700 BC → c. AD 95 (The Grand Inclusio)

ot.author: Moses, Isaiah & Ezekiel
ot.context: The Tree of Life in Eden, Isaiah's prophecy of New Heavens and a New Earth, and Ezekiel's vision of the healing river flowing from the Temple.
ot.text: Out of the ground the LORD God gave growth to every tree that is pleasing to the eye and good for food. And in the middle of the garden were the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. … For behold, I will create new heavens and a new earth. The former things will not be remembered, nor will they come to mind. … Then the man brought me back to the entrance of the temple, and I saw water flowing from under the threshold of the temple toward the east (for the temple faced east). The water was coming down from under the south side of the temple, south of the altar. Next he brought me out through the north gate and led me around the outside to the outer gate facing east, and there I saw the water trickling out from the south side. As the man went eastward with a measuring line in his hand, he measured off a thousand cubits and led me through ankle-deep water. Then he measured off a thousand cubits and led me through knee-deep water. Again he measured a thousand cubits and led me through waist-deep water. Once again he measured off a thousand cubits, but now it was a river that I could not cross, because the water had risen and was deep enough for swimming—a river that could not be crossed on foot. “Son of man, do you see this?” he asked. Then he led me back to the bank of the river. When I arrived, I saw a great number of trees along both banks of the river. And he said to me, “This water flows out to the eastern region and goes down into the Arabah. When it empties into the Sea, the water there becomes fresh. Wherever the river flows, there will be swarms of living creatures and a great number of fish, because it flows there and makes the waters fresh; so wherever the river flows, everything will flourish. Fishermen will stand by the shore; from En-gedi to En-eglaim they will spread their nets to catch fish of many kinds, like the fish of the Great Sea. But the swamps and marshes will not become fresh; they will be left for salt. Along both banks of the river, fruit trees of all kinds will grow. Their leaves will not wither, and their fruit will not fail. Each month they will bear fruit, because the water from the sanctuary flows to them. Their fruit will be used for food and their leaves for healing.”
ot.keyPhrase: I will create new heavens and a new earth

nt.author: John
nt.context: John's closing vision: a new heaven and a new earth, God dwelling with His people, the river of the water of life, the tree of life, and no more curse.
nt.text: Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and earth had passed away, and the sea was no more. I saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband. And I heard a loud voice from the throne saying: “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them. They will be His people, and God Himself will be with them as their God. ‘He will wipe away every tear from their eyes,’ and there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain, for the former things have passed away.” And the One seated on the throne said, “Behold, I make all things new.” Then He said, “Write this down, for these words are faithful and true.” … Then the angel showed me a river of the water of life, as clear as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb down the middle of the main street of the city. On either side of the river stood a tree of life, bearing twelve kinds of fruit and yielding a fresh crop for each month. And the leaves of the tree are for the healing of the nations. No longer will there be any curse. The throne of God and of the Lamb will be within the city, and His servants will worship Him. They will see His face, and His name will be on their foreheads. There will be no more night in the city, and they will have no need for the light of a lamp or of the sun. For the Lord God will shine on them, and they will reign forever and ever.
nt.keyPhrase: Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth

bridge: Revelation never introduces a formal quotation, but its closing vision is built from Old Testament words. 'A new heaven and a new earth' takes up Isaiah 65:17. The river flowing from God's throne, lined by the tree of life with fruit each month and leaves 'for the healing of the nations', closely follows Ezekiel's river from the temple, whose trees also bear fruit every month and have leaves for healing (Ezekiel 47:12). The tree of life, guarded since Eden (Genesis 2:9; 3:24), stands again by the river, and 'no longer will there be any curse'. Many readers see here a frame around the whole Bible, an inclusio (a story that ends where it began): what was lost in Genesis 3 is restored, and more, through the Lamb.

title: God's Covenant with David & the Son's Eternal Throne

ot.author: The Chronicler (traditionally Ezra)
ot.context: God's covenant promise to David through Nathan, given when David wants to build a house for God (1 Chronicles 17:1-4).
ot.text: And when your days are fulfilled and you go to be with your fathers, I will raise up your descendant after you, one of your own sons, and I will establish his kingdom. He will build a house for Me, and I will establish his throne forever. I will be his Father, and he will be My son. And I will never remove My loving devotion from him as I removed it from your predecessor. But I will set him over My house and My kingdom forever, and his throne will be established forever.”
ot.keyPhrase: I will be his Father, and he will be My son

nt.author: Author of Hebrews / Luke
nt.context: Hebrews 1 quoting the promise to David to show that the Son is greater than the angels; the angel's words to Mary in Luke 1.
nt.text: For to which of the angels did God ever say: “You are My Son; today I have become Your Father”? Or again: “I will be His Father, and He will be My Son”? … He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High. The Lord God will give Him the throne of His father David, and He will reign over the house of Jacob forever. His kingdom will never end!”
nt.keyPhrase: I will be His Father, and He will be My Son

bridge: When David wants to build a house for God (1 Chronicles 17:1-4), God promises instead to raise up David's descendant and 'establish his throne forever'. Hebrews 1:5 quotes 'I will be His Father, and He will be My Son' and applies it to Jesus, to show that He is greater than the angels. Luke 1:32-33 echoes the same promise: Jesus will receive 'the throne of His father David', and 'His kingdom will never end!' The version in 1 Chronicles leaves out a line found in 2 Samuel 7:14: 'When he does wrong, I will discipline him'. Many readers see this as keeping attention on the lasting promise, which suits the way Hebrews applies it to Christ.

title: From the Blood of Abel to the Blood of Zechariah

ot.author: The Chronicler (traditionally Ezra)
ot.context: King Joash has the priest Zechariah son of Jehoiada stoned in the temple courtyard for rebuking the people; dying, Zechariah asks the LORD to see and call them to account.
ot.text: Then the Spirit of God came upon Zechariah son of Jehoiada the priest, who stood up before the people and said to them, “This is what God says: ‘Why do you transgress the commandments of the LORD so that you cannot prosper? Because you have forsaken the LORD, He has forsaken you.’” But they conspired against Zechariah, and by order of the king, they stoned him in the courtyard of the house of the LORD. Thus King Joash failed to remember the kindness that Zechariah’s father Jehoiada had extended to him. Instead, Joash killed Jehoiada’s son. As he lay dying, Zechariah said, “May the LORD see this and call you to account.”
ot.keyPhrase: they stoned him in the courtyard of the house of the LORD

nt.author: Matthew / Luke
nt.context: Jesus indicting the religious leaders for the blood of all the prophets from Abel (Genesis) to Zechariah (2 Chronicles).
nt.text: And so upon you will come all the righteous blood shed on earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Berechiah, whom you murdered between the temple and the altar. … As a result, this generation will be charged with the blood of all the prophets that has been shed since the foundation of the world, from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah, who was killed between the altar and the sanctuary. Yes, I tell you, all of it will be charged to this generation.
nt.keyPhrase: the blood of Zechariah, who was killed between the altar and the sanctuary

bridge: Jesus warns that 'this generation will be charged with the blood of all the prophets', from Abel, the first murder victim (Genesis 4:8), to Zechariah, killed 'between the altar and the sanctuary'. He is recalling, not quoting, the death of the priest Zechariah, whom King Joash had stoned in the temple courtyard and who died saying, 'May the LORD see this and call you to account.' Because Chronicles stands last in the traditional order of the Hebrew Bible, many think 'from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah' spans all of Scripture, first martyr to last, though we cannot be sure that order was fixed in Jesus' day. Matthew calls this Zechariah 'son of Berechiah', the name of the later prophet's father (Zechariah 1:1), while Chronicles has 'son of Jehoiada', a long-discussed difficulty.

title: The Breath of the Lord Slaying the Lawless One

ot.author: Isaiah
ot.context: The promised shoot from the stump of Jesse (Isaiah 11:1) judges with righteousness and slays the wicked with the breath of His lips; the LORD comes with fire to judge.
ot.text: but with righteousness He will judge the poor, and with equity He will decide for the lowly of the earth. He will strike the earth with the rod of His mouth and slay the wicked with the breath of His lips. … For behold, the LORD will come with fire— His chariots are like a whirlwind— to execute His anger with fury and His rebuke with flames of fire.
ot.keyPhrase: slay the wicked with the breath of His lips

nt.author: Paul
nt.context: Paul describes the Lord Jesus revealed from heaven in blazing fire and destroying the lawless one at His coming.
nt.text: And then the lawless one will be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus will slay with the breath of His mouth and annihilate by the majesty of His arrival. … and to grant relief to you who are oppressed and to us as well. This will take place when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven with His mighty angels in blazing fire, inflicting vengeance on those who do not know God and do not obey the gospel of our Lord Jesus.
nt.keyPhrase: whom the Lord Jesus will slay with the breath of His mouth

bridge: Isaiah 11 promises a descendant of Jesse, David's father (Isaiah 11:1), who will judge the poor with righteousness and 'slay the wicked with the breath of His lips'. In 2 Thessalonians 2:8 Paul applies the same picture to the Lord Jesus at His coming: He 'will slay with the breath of His mouth' the lawless one, the 'man of lawlessness' Paul has just described (2 Thessalonians 2:3-4). Paul does not introduce the words as Scripture and says 'mouth' for 'lips', so this is a strong allusion (borrowed wording not marked as a quotation) rather than a formal quotation. Likewise 2 Thessalonians 1:7-8 pictures Jesus revealed 'in blazing fire, inflicting vengeance', which echoes Isaiah 66:15, where the LORD comes with fire.

title: 'Charge It to My Account': Intercession & Imputation

ot.author: Moses & Isaiah
ot.context: Judah offers to stay in Egypt as a slave in place of Benjamin; Isaiah's Servant bears the iniquities of others.
ot.text: Indeed, your servant guaranteed the boy’s safety to my father, saying, ‘If I do not return him to you, I will bear the guilt before you, my father, all my life.’ Now please let your servant stay here as my lord’s slave in place of the boy. Let him return with his brothers. … We all like sheep have gone astray, each one has turned to his own way; and the LORD has laid upon Him the iniquity of us all. … After the anguish of His soul, He will see the light of life and be satisfied. By His knowledge My righteous Servant will justify many, and He will bear their iniquities.
ot.keyPhrase: the LORD has laid upon Him the iniquity of us all

nt.author: Paul
nt.context: Paul asks Philemon to receive Onesimus as he would receive Paul himself and offers to repay anything he owes; he also writes that God made Christ 'to be sin on our behalf'.
nt.text: So if you consider me a partner, receive him as you would receive me. But if he has wronged you in any way or owes you anything, charge it to my account. I, Paul, write this with my own hand. I will repay it—not to mention that you owe me your very self. … God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God.
nt.keyPhrase: if he has wronged you in any way or owes you anything, charge it to my account

bridge: When Benjamin is about to be kept as a slave in Egypt, Judah pleads for him and offers to take his place: 'Now please let your servant stay here as my lord’s slave in place of the boy.' Paul pleads for Onesimus in a similar way, writing to Philemon: 'If he has wronged you in any way or owes you anything, charge it to my account.' Nothing in Philemon points back to Judah or to Isaiah; the two stories share only the idea of one person standing in for another.
